recipes.name: Let the compiler infer Send and Sync: they turn data races into E0277/E0499, not race conditions or deadlocks
recipes.what: Send and Sync are unsafe auto traits derived from a type's fields. An Rc or raw-pointer field stops a value moving to another thread and a Cell field stops it being shared (both E0277), and two threads writing one variable fail with E0499. A check-then-act on atomics still loses updates.
recipes.how: Read Send as 'ownership may move to another thread' and Sync as '&T may be shared' (T: Sync exactly when &T: Send). The compiler implements both for a struct, enum, tuple or closure when every field or capture has them. The usual non-thread-safe leaves: Rc (neither), Cell / RefCell / UnsafeCell (Send when T: Send, never Sync, so &Cell<T> is not Send), *const T / *mut T (neither), NonNull (not Send), MutexGuard (not Send). Answer E0277 'cannot be sent/shared between threads safely' by changing the type: Rc -> Arc, Cell / RefCell -> an atomic, Mutex or RwLock, a raw-pointer view -> an owned buffer or an index. `unsafe impl Send` is a promise you prove (the Rustonomicon's Carton shows the reasoning), and `impl !Send` is nightly-only. The compiler does not catch race conditions: make each check-then-act one atomic read-modify-write (fetch_add, compare_exchange) or hold one lock across it.
recipes.rust_version: any; the disjoint-field closure capture in the gotcha is edition 2021+
recipes.gotchas: Edition 2021 closures capture disjoint fields: `move || v.len` captures only the usize, so a struct holding a *mut f64 crosses a thread boundary while only Send fields are used and fails E0277 the day an edit touches the pointer (both checks below). E0277's headline names the leaf type (`*mut f64`, `&Cell<u32>`); only the notes below it walk back to your struct. 'Safe Rust has no data races' does not mean 'no races': the Rustonomicon calls race conditions and deadlocks safe; the forced interleaving below loses an update with nothing but atomics.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs exports raw `*mut f64` from `bodies_ptr()` and `colliders_ptr()`. Any Rust-side host wrapper that stores those pointers is automatically neither Send nor Sync. That is the compiler enforcing one-thread use of the static buffers, so keep it rather than adding `unsafe impl Send`.
recipes.verify_note: Send/Sync/Nomicon/Reference/Book quotes match claims verbatim. All 6 checks (3xE0277, E0499, 2 runs) recompiled/ran exactly as specified on rustc 1.98.1. bodies_ptr/colliders_ptr *mut f64 confirmed live in lib.rs via gh api.

sources.title: The Rustonomicon: Data Races and Race Conditions
sources.claim: Safe Rust guarantees the absence of data races but does not prevent general race conditions, and deadlocks and race conditions are 'safe' because they cannot violate memory safety alone.

sources.title: The Rustonomicon: Send and Sync
sources.claim: Send and Sync are derived automatically; raw pointers are neither, UnsafeCell (so Cell and RefCell) is not Sync, Rc is neither, and a manual unsafe impl must be justified as in the Carton example; impl !Send needs the nightly negative_impls feature.

recipes.name: Borrow stack data in worker threads with thread::scope (1.63); thread::spawn needs move and 'static
recipes.what: std::thread::spawn requires F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static, so a closure borrowing a local is E0373, while std::thread::scope (stable 1.63.0) joins every scoped thread before returning, so workers can borrow slices and write disjoint chunks without Arc.
recipes.how: For a detached or long-lived worker use `thread::spawn(move || ...)` and get the result back with `JoinHandle::join()`, which returns `Err(payload)` when that thread panicked (under panic = unwind only that thread unwinds). For fork-join work over data you own, use `thread::scope(|s| { for (src, dst) in input.chunks(n).zip(out.chunks_mut(n)) { s.spawn(move || ...); } })`: shared `&[T]` reads and disjoint `&mut [T]` writes, no Arc and no 'static. Join a `ScopedJoinHandle` inside the scope when a worker's panic should become a value; otherwise `scope` re-raises it after joining. Use `thread::Builder::new().spawn(..)` (or `spawn_scoped`, 1.63.0) when a failure to create a thread must be an `io::Result`, not a panic.
recipes.rust_version: 1.63+ for thread::scope and Builder::spawn_scoped; thread::spawn any
recipes.gotchas: Adding `move` to silence E0373 moves the Vec into one thread, so a second worker cannot use it; scoped threads share it without Arc. Dropping a JoinHandle detaches the thread, and when main returns the process ends and detached threads are shut down. `thread::scope` panics in the caller if an un-joined scoped thread panicked (exit 101 below), which kills a sweep that meant to record the failure. Thread-local destructors of scoped threads may still be running after `scope` returns.
recipes.engine_note: The offline tools around the law (Phase 2 T5 nightly replay corpus, T6 reachability sweep) can fan work out with scoped threads, but not by calling one native law from several threads: the solver keeps its world in process-global `static mut` state (lib.rs `BODIES` / `COLLIDERS`, rapier_law.rs `SOLVER`). Run one law per process.
recipes.verify_note: thread::scope/spawn/Builder docs match verbatim incl. the thread-local-destructor caveat. All 4 checks compiled/ran as specified. static mut BODIES/COLLIDERS(lib.rs)/SOLVER(rapier_law.rs) confirmed via gh api.

recipes.name: Pick Mutex, RwLock or Condvar by job, and decide what a poisoned lock means before a panic decides for you
recipes.what: Mutex<T> hands one thread &mut T at a time; RwLock<T> allows many readers or one writer under an OS-dependent priority policy; Condvar::wait_while sleeps until a predicate over the guarded state holds; a panic while holding a Mutex (or an RwLock in write mode) poisons it, and poisoning is only advisory.
recipes.how: Mutex for state every user mutates; RwLock only for read-mostly state, and never re-lock it on the thread that holds it; Condvar for 'wait until the state says X', always `cv.wait_while(lock.lock().unwrap(), |s| !ready(s))` (1.42.0), never a bare `wait`, because wakeups can be spurious and notify_one / notify_all are not buffered. Keep each guard in the smallest block, never call unknown code while holding one, and take several locks in one fixed global order. Decide poisoning per lock: `match m.lock() { Ok(g) => .., Err(p) => refuse or repair via p.into_inner() }`, then `m.clear_poison()` (1.77.0) once the invariant is restored. Detect a same-thread relock with `try_lock()`: it returns `TryLockError::WouldBlock` where `lock()` would never return.
recipes.gotchas: `.lock().unwrap()` everywhere turns one panic into a panic in every thread that touches the lock; the docs describe that propagation as the default intent, so choose it deliberately. Relocking a Mutex on the holding thread is unspecified and never returns (panic or deadlock). A waiting writer may block new readers, so a recursive `read()` can deadlock. A reader's panic does not poison an RwLock. Unsafe code cannot rely on poisoning for soundness: some panics (a second panic inside Drop, foreign exceptions) leave a mutex unpoisoned. On 1.98.1 the non-poisoning locks (`std::sync::nonpoison`) are still experimental. Under panic = "abort" a panic ends the process, so no survivor ever sees a poisoned lock.
recipes.engine_note: If a native host puts the law behind a Mutex (see the native-call recipe), a poisoned law lock means the world may be half-stepped. Refuse the call and return 0, as the exports already do for NaN, instead of stepping on from `into_inner()`. The solver's release profile (`panic = "abort"` in solver/Cargo.toml) ends the process on a panic, so poisoning only arises in unwind builds such as tests.
recipes.verify_note: Mutex/RwLock/Condvar docs confirm poisoning, writer-only RwLock poisoning, spurious wakeups, non-buffered notify, incl. 'unsafe cannot rely on poisoning'. All 4 checks ran as specified. panic="abort" confirmed in Cargo.toml.

recipes.name: Hand results between threads over mpsc or crossbeam channels and sort by a tag: arrival order is scheduling
recipes.what: std::sync::mpsc offers an unbounded channel() and a bounded sync_channel(n) (n = 0 is a rendezvous); iterating the Receiver ends only after every Sender is dropped; with several producers the arrival order depends on scheduling, so tag each message and sort before the data reaches a hash or a report.
recipes.how: `let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();` clone `tx` per producer, `drop(tx)` the original, then `for msg in rx` or `rx.iter().collect()`. Send `(index, value)` and `sort_by_key(|&(i, _)| i)` before folding or hashing. Use `sync_channel(k)` for back-pressure: senders block when k messages are queued and `try_send` returns `TrySendError::Full(v)`; `sync_channel(0)` hands a value over only when a receiver is waiting. Disconnection is a value, not a panic: send fails once the receiver is gone, recv fails once all senders are gone. Since 1.67.0 std's mpsc is built on crossbeam-channel, and Sender is Sync since 1.72.0. For several consumers or `select!` over channels and timers, use crossbeam-channel 0.5.17 (`bounded`, `unbounded`, zero-capacity, `select!`, `after` / `tick`), because `std::sync::mpmc` is still unstable on 1.98.1 (E0658, feature `mpmc_channel`).
recipes.rust_version: any; Sender: Sync 1.72+; std::sync::mpmc unstable on 1.98.1; crossbeam-channel 0.5.17
recipes.gotchas: Forgetting `drop(tx)` makes `for msg in rx` block forever. That is a hang, not an error. FIFO holds per channel in send order, not in the order the producers were spawned. `Ok` from `send` does not mean the value was received. Reaching for std's mpmc on stable fails to compile.
recipes.engine_note: Tools that spread runs of the law across workers (T5 nightly replay corpus, T6 reachability sweep) should send `(run_index, trace_hash)` and sort by run_index before writing the report. The report is then byte-stable and diffable like the golden hashes it summarises.

recipes.name: Publish data across threads with a Release store and an Acquire load; keep Relaxed for counters
recipes.what: Rust atomics follow the C++20 model: a Release store paired with an Acquire load of the same atomic makes every earlier write visible after the load, Relaxed only makes each operation atomic, SeqCst adds one total order, and an ordering an operation cannot take is a deny-by-default lint (or a run-time panic when it arrives in a variable).
recipes.how: Message passing: the writer does `DATA.store(x, Relaxed); READY.store(true, Release);` and the reader does `while !READY.load(Acquire) { std::hint::spin_loop() }` then `DATA.load(Relaxed)`. Counters and statistics: `fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` never loses an increment. A busy flag: `compare_exchange(false, true, Acquire, Relaxed)` to enter and `store(false, Release)` to leave (the check runs it as a wasm32-unknown-unknown export, where atomics build without the `atomics` feature). Use SeqCst when several flags must be seen in one global order, or whenever you are unsure. Loads cannot be Release or AcqRel, stores cannot be Acquire or AcqRel, fences cannot be Relaxed, and a compare-exchange failure ordering cannot be Release or AcqRel: `invalid_atomic_ordering` rejects literals. std has no AtomicF64 (E0432): keep an f64 in an `AtomicU64` via `to_bits` / `f64::from_bits`.
recipes.gotchas: x86 is strongly ordered, so a Relaxed-where-Acquire-was-needed bug usually passes tests there; the Rustonomicon says to test concurrent algorithms on weakly-ordered hardware (ARM). Release on a read-modify-write gives a Relaxed load half, so use AcqRel when the RMW both publishes and consumes. An ordering passed through a variable escapes the lint and panics at run time. A data race (conflicting non-synchronized accesses, at least one non-atomic) is undefined behaviour even when the output looks right.
recipes.engine_note: The law needs no atomics: one thread, and wasm32-unknown-unknown without the `atomics` feature. Host or tool code that uses them should also run its tests on the Phase-2 T3 ARM64 lane, where a too-weak ordering can show up that x86 hides.
recipes.verify_note: Ordering/atomic/Nomicon/lint docs confirm the C++20 model and lint scope verbatim. All 6 checks compiled/ran incl. runtime-panic-via-variable and the wasm32 compare_exchange case (wasm_no_imports gate holds).

recipes.name: Make parallel float reductions bit-reproducible: fixed chunks, per-chunk partials, combined in index order
recipes.what: Float addition is not associative, so a parallel sum's bits depend on where the input is split and how the partials are combined. rayon's sum, reduce and fold leave that order unspecified (fold's docs call its break points nondeterministic), so results can change between runs and thread counts. A chunk size fixed in the code, with partials folded sequentially in chunk order, gives the same bits for any thread count.
recipes.how: Treat the reduction tree as part of the computation: a constant chunk size (never derived from the thread count or `available_parallelism()`), a sequential sum inside each chunk, each partial stored at its chunk index, then one sequential fold over the partials in index order. With std: `thread::scope` plus `partials.chunks_mut(per_thread)`. With rayon 1.12.0: fixed-size `par_chunks(CHUNK)` / `fold_chunks` producing partials that you combine yourself in index order; do not call `.sum()` or `.reduce()` on floats and expect stable bits. This is the pattern Rapier 0.35.3 uses in its parallel body-update pass (`par_chunks(256)`, results combined in order). rayon's reduce contract asks for an associative op; float `+` is not one, while wrapping integer addition is.
recipes.rust_version: any; rayon claims per rayon 1.12.0 / rayon-core 1.13.0
recipes.gotchas: The fixed-chunk result is reproducible across thread counts but is generally not the bits of the plain sequential sum (the check prints false), so changing CHUNK changes the result and must be treated like any other change to the computation. 'Same input on the same machine' is not enough under rayon: its docs call fold's break points nondeterministic, and join runs on work stealing. On wasm32-unknown-unknown rayon quietly falls back to a single-threaded mode, so a parallel float reduction there can give different bits from the same code on a native host.
recipes.engine_note: Inside the wasm law nothing is reduced in parallel: Rapier runs its staged solver with one worker when `parallel` is off. The rule binds tools that aggregate floats across runs (T5 corpus statistics, T6 sweep metrics) and any future native build that turns rapier's `parallel` on.

recipes.name: Keep the wasm law single-threaded: no threads on wasm32-unknown-unknown, rapier3d-f64's parallel left off
recipes.what: On wasm32-unknown-unknown, std::thread::spawn panics (Builder::spawn returns Err) and available_parallelism errs. Shared-memory threads need the unstable `atomics` target feature plus a core and std rebuilt with it (nightly -Zbuild-std): stable 1.98.1's shipped core and std refuse --shared-memory at link time. Rapier 0.35.3 declares no conflict between `parallel` and `enhanced-determinism`, and its changelog says they 'can now be combined' with bitwise-identical results for any pool size.
recipes.how: Probe a target instead of assuming: `std::thread::Builder::new().spawn(..).is_err()`, `std::thread::available_parallelism().is_err()` and `cfg!(target_feature = "atomics")` are 1, 1 and 0 on wasm32-unknown-unknown (checks). Threaded wasm needs `-C target-feature=+atomics,+bulk-memory,+mutable-globals` with `cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=panic_abort,std`, or the experimental wasm32-wasip1-threads target (wasi-threads; links with --shared-memory, --import-memory and --export-memory). For Rapier, read the feature table at the pinned version: at 0.35.3 `parallel = ["dep:rayon", "std", "parry3d-f64/parallel"]`, `enhanced-determinism = ["simba/libm_force", "parry3d-f64/enhanced-determinism"]`, and the only compile_error! pairs `simd8` (an f32-only feature that rapier3d-f64 does not declare) with enhanced-determinism. With `parallel` off, `rapier3d_f64::rayon` and `PhysicsPipeline::configure_thread_pool` do not exist (checks). Rapier's `PhysicsHooks` and `EventHandler` require Sync even with `parallel` off (unless `unsync-callbacks`): hook state goes in atomics, not Cell. Features unify across a build graph, so any crate enabling `rapier3d-f64/parallel` turns it on for everyone; watch it with `cargo tree -e features -i rapier3d-f64`.
recipes.gotchas: Stale advice: 'enhanced-determinism is incompatible with parallel'. Rapier's v0.35.0-beta.0 changelog says the two 'can now be combined' with bitwise-identical results for any thread-pool size, and its current user guide (labelled 0.36) says the same. That is the vendor's claim, not measured here, and the same release's notes say multithreaded trajectories may shift within solver tolerance after the solver rewrite. On stable, `+atomics` only earns the warning 'unstable feature specified for `-Ctarget-feature`: `atomics`' and then a link error, even for a `#![no_std]` module, because core itself was not compiled with atomics. rayon on this target silently runs single-threaded, and its `spawn` may never run.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml turns on only `enhanced-determinism` for rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 (defaults dim3, f64, std, block-solver; `parallel` off, as solver/FLAGS.md records). Keep it off in the wasm law: the target has no threads to use, and the feature compiles rayon and the parallel code paths into the module whose bytes fixtures/solver.sha256 pins. If a native Godot or Unreal build ever turns `parallel` on, re-measure the golden hash at several thread-pool sizes before trusting Rapier's bitwise claim, and add a CI feature guard (owned by ci-reproducible-builds).

True of wasi-threads generally, not sourced on this page.

recipes.name: Serialize native calls into the law: static needs Sync, static mut skips the check, a Mutex restores it
recipes.what: A plain static must be Sync (E0277 'shared static variables must have a type that implements `Sync`') but a static mut is exempt, so a static-mut world compiles with no thread-safety check at all. A native host must own the law on one thread or put it behind a static Mutex, which compiles because rapier3d-f64 0.35.3's PhysicsWorld and KinematicCharacterController are Send. LazyLock (1.80) and OnceLock (1.70) cover read-only globals.
recipes.how: Hold the mutable world as `static LAW: Mutex<Option<Law>> = Mutex::new(None);` (`Mutex::new` is const since 1.63; `Mutex<T>` is Sync when T is Send), or hand the host an owned handle instead of globals. Make every export refuse instead of block: `match LAW.try_lock() { Ok(mut law) => step(&mut law), Err(TryLockError::WouldBlock) | Err(TryLockError::Poisoned(_)) => 0 }`. That keeps the exports' u32 1/0 convention for re-entrant or concurrent calls and for a law that panicked mid-step. The same Mutex compiles for wasm32-unknown-unknown and imports nothing (check), so one source serves both targets. For read-only tables built once, use `static T: LazyLock<Vec<f64>> = LazyLock::new(|| ..)` (the initializer runs once even with 8 racing threads) or `OnceLock::get_or_init`; `OnceLock::set` returns `Err(value)` after the first set, and `get_or_try_init` is nightly-only. How to rewrite `static mut` references soundly is the unsafe-ffi lane's recipe.
recipes.gotchas: Swapping `static mut` for `thread_local!` gives every calling thread its own world, which diverges silently (check). A LazyLock whose initializer panicked is poisoned for good: every later access panics, with no into_inner escape (check), so never put fallible I/O in its initializer. `static mut` compiles with any type because the compiler checks nothing there. The single-thread assumption then lives only in comments.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs holds `static mut BODIES` and `COLLIDERS` (f64 arrays); solver/src/rapier_law.rs holds `static mut HEIGHTS` and `static mut SOLVER: Solver` (the loaded PhysicsWorld, controller and snapshot Vec). The types are Sync (f64 arrays trivially, PhysicsWorld per the check). What two host threads would break is the unsynchronized mutation that `static mut` allows: a data race, which is UB. `solver_clear_warmstart` even notes 'The world is ours alone on this thread', which nothing enforces. In the wasm module the JS host calls exports one at a time. Compiled natively for a Godot or Unreal host, two threads calling `solver_step` would race. Move the state into one `static LAW: Mutex<Option<Loaded>>` (or a host-owned handle) and have each export try_lock and return 0 on WouldBlock or Poisoned.
recipes.verify_note: Reference/Mutex/LazyLock/OnceLock docs confirm static-Sync exemption, poisoning, once-init verbatim. All 9 checks incl. no_warnings/wasm_no_imports gates passed. static mut fields + 'world is ours alone' quote confirmed via gh api.

recipes.name: Treat a future as an inert, pinned state machine: nothing runs until polled, and dropping it cancels it
recipes.what: Calling an async fn only builds a future, a compiler-generated state machine that stores every local alive across an .await. Nothing runs until an executor polls it through Pin<&mut Self>; async-block futures are !Unpin and must be pinned (pin!, 1.68, or Box::pin). Dropping a pending future runs its destructors, and the code after its current .await never executes.
recipes.how: Always `.await` or hand the future to an executor: a bare `step();` is only an `unused_must_use` warning ('futures do nothing unless you `.await` or poll them'), and the body never runs. Rust ships no runtime. Use tokio (or another executor) in programs; in tests, a 10-line `block_on` with `pin!(fut)` and `Context::from_waker(Waker::noop())` (1.85) is enough for futures that finish without waiting on I/O. `Pin::new(&mut fut)` on an async block is E0277 'cannot be unpinned'; the compiler's note says to use `pin!`, or `Box::pin` when the pinned future must outlive the scope. Keep big temporaries out of the state machine by ending their scope before the .await (a 4 KiB buffer held across an await makes the future at least 4096 bytes). Cancellation is drop: tokio's `select!` cancels the losing branches, and a future is cancellation-safe when dropping and recreating it is a no-op. Put cleanup in Drop guards, not after an .await.
recipes.gotchas: A `Waker::noop` busy-poll loop is for tests only: it discards wake-ups, so a future waiting on I/O would spin. Polling a future again after it returned Ready may panic or block. Code after an .await is not guaranteed to run, because an executor, a timeout or `select!` may drop the future at that point (the drop check shows 'after await' never printed).
recipes.engine_note: The law's exports (`step`, `solver_load`, `solver_step`, `solver_clear_warmstart`) are synchronous and CPU-bound, driven by the JS tick at 1/64 s. A quantum has no I/O to wait on, so the law gains nothing from async. Async belongs, if anywhere, in host and tool I/O around the law.

recipes.name: Spawn only Send + 'static futures: no std MutexGuard or Rc across .await, CPU-bound work to spawn_blocking
recipes.what: tokio::spawn (1.53.1) requires F: Future + Send + 'static because a task can move between worker threads. A std MutexGuard or Rc alive across an .await makes the future !Send; on 1.98.1 the error 'future cannot be sent between threads safely' carries no error code. Blocking or long CPU work belongs on spawn_blocking or rayon. Async closures (1.85) are for callbacks awaited in place.
recipes.how: Before an .await, end every guard's scope with an inner block `{ let mut g = m.lock().unwrap(); ... }`, a one-statement temporary (`*m.lock().unwrap() += 1;`), or a plain sync helper function. Not touching the guard after the await is not enough, because it still drops at the end of its scope. On 1.98.1 `drop(g)` is not enough either once `g` has been used through Deref: the compiler still reports it 'maybe used later' (check). The std Mutex stays the default for data in async code (tokio's own docs); `tokio::sync::Mutex` is for holding a lock across .await, typically an I/O resource. Tokio switches tasks only at .await, so CPU-bound or blocking calls go to `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (not abortable) or a rayon pool. A dropped `JoinHandle` detaches its task; `abort()` cancels it. For callbacks awaited in place, take `impl AsyncFn(..)` / `AsyncFnMut` / `AsyncFnOnce` and pass `async |x| ..`. These traits are in the prelude (the edition-2021 check needs no import), and the returned future may borrow the closure's captures, which `FnMut(u32) -> Fut` with `|x| async { v.push(x) }` cannot express.
recipes.gotchas: Search logs for the text 'future cannot be sent between threads safely', not for E0277: the compiler emits no error code for it. The common advice 'call drop(guard) before the .await' fails on 1.98.1 as soon as the guard was used through Deref, even for a read (checks). Scope it instead. The old `|x| async { .. }` callback fails with 'captured variable cannot escape `FnMut` closure body' (plus E0373), and `async move` inside it only changes that to E0507. A borrowing async closure's future borrows the closure itself, so it can be awaited but not spawned (E0597, check). Dropping a JoinHandle does not cancel the task.
recipes.engine_note: A tokio-based host or tool (a replay service, an asset server) should call the law through `spawn_blocking` or one dedicated law thread fed by a channel, because the law is CPU-bound and process-global. It must never hold the law's std MutexGuard across an .await.

recipes.what: macro_rules! matches token fragments under follow-set rules and mixed-site hygiene, is visible only after its definition unless #[macro_export] moves it to the crate root, and from edition 2024 `expr` also matches `const { }` and `_` while `expr_2021` keeps the 2021 set.
recipes.how: Fragments on 1.98.1 (Reference): block, expr, expr_2021, ident, item, lifetime, literal, meta, pat, pat_param, path, stmt, tt, ty, vis. Repetition is `$( ... ) sep op` with `*`, `+` or `?` (`?` takes no separator); end a list with `$(,)?` to accept a trailing comma. `expr` and `stmt` may be followed only by `=>`, `,` or `;`, so `($e:expr $i:ident)` is rejected where the macro is defined. Locals and labels created inside an expansion are invisible to the caller (E0425, 'not accessible due to macro hygiene'); other names resolve at the call site. A macro enters textual scope after its definition; `#[macro_export]` makes it pub at the crate root (`crate::slot!`, `other_crate::slot!`), so name every item the expansion uses as `$crate::module::item`. Edition 2024: for `example!(const { 1 + 1 })` the same two-arm macro prints 'second rule' in 2021 and 'first rule' in 2024; `m!(_)` goes to the `tt` arm in 2021 and the `expr` arm in 2024; `expr_2021` (stable in every edition since 1.83) restores the 2021 set, and the `edition_2024_expr_fragment_specifier` lint that `cargo fix --edition` applies rewrites `expr` to `expr_2021`. For ABI numbers use `$v:literal`, which no edition changes. Use macro_rules! to declare items (consts, exports, impls) or to name them with `stringify!`; compute values with const fn.
recipes.rust_version: any; expr_2021 1.83+; the wider expr is edition 2024 only
recipes.gotchas: Arms are tried in order and the first match wins, so an `expr` arm placed before a `const`-prefixed arm silently changes which arm fires when the crate moves to 2024. `cargo fix --edition` turns every `expr` into `expr_2021`: behaviour-preserving, but it hides whether the new meaning was wanted. `#[macro_export]` ignores the defining module's path (the macro lives at the crate root); `local_inner_macros` exists for pre-$crate code and is discouraged in new code. Invoking a macro above its definition fails with 'cannot find macro' (rustc notes that one exists later); a non-exported macro inside `mod abi` is invisible outside it unless the module carries `#[macro_use]`. Diagnostics point into expansions, so keep macro bodies to declarations and call functions for logic.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs and rapier_law.rs (e5fbcb9) contain no macro_rules! today. The first one that earns its place is the ABI table (see 'Pin the solver ABI with const _ assertions...'): one invocation declaring BODY_STRIDE, HX..DRIVEN and COLLIDER_STRIDE plus their stringify!'d names. The solver crate is edition 2021, so write `$v:literal` (or `expr_2021`) there: an `expr` fragment written today would widen on a 2024 migration.

recipes.name: Use a derive proc macro only when code must read a type's definition; count its syn builds in build time
recipes.what: Proc macros (derive, attribute, function-like) live in separate proc-macro crates that rustc runs during expansion, usually on syn, quote and proc-macro2; they can generate code and compile-time checks from a struct's definition, and they cost host-side dependency builds plus unoptimized expansion (uncached, per the 2025 survey post).
recipes.how: Kinds (Reference): `#[proc_macro]` for `name!(...)`, `#[proc_macro_derive(Name, attributes(helper))]` for `#[derive(Name)]`, `#[proc_macro_attribute]` for `#[name]`; they must sit at the root of a crate with `proc-macro = true` and can be used only from another crate. The usual stack: syn parses the TokenStream into a syntax tree (default features derive, parsing, printing, clone-impls, proc-macro; `full`, `visit`, `fold` are opt-in because syn is 'aggressively feature gated'), `quote!` turns syntax back into tokens (`#var`, `#(...)*`), and proc-macro2 wraps the compiler's proc_macro types so the same code also runs in build scripts and unit tests. Cargo builds build scripts, proc macros and their dependencies with `build-override` `opt-level = 0`, `codegen-units = 256` in dev and in release. Measured cost (`cargo +1.98.1 build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --offline --locked --timings` on a scratch copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9, cold, 24 jobs): 66 units in 30.6 s; syn 2.0.119 (1.95 s) and syn 3.0.6 (1.38 s) compiled in parallel, then thiserror-impl 0.65 s, num-derive 0.56 s, nalgebra-macros 0.31 s, profiling-procmacros 0.25 s, all done by about 3.8 s and off the critical path wide (5.7 s) -> simba -> nalgebra (4.7 s) -> parry3d-f64 (12.1 s) -> rapier3d-f64 (15.3 s). Choose macro_rules! when the input is tokens written at the call site; choose a derive when the code must read fields and repr. Example: bytemuck's `#[derive(Pod)]` fails a padded `#[repr(C)]` struct with E0080 and lets `bytemuck::cast_slice` view `[Body]` as `[f64]` without unsafe.
recipes.rust_version: any; as locked: syn 2.0.119 and 3.0.6, quote 1.0.47, proc-macro2 1.0.107, bytemuck 1.25.2
recipes.gotchas: Proc macros are unhygienic: their output behaves as if typed at the use site, so it can capture or clash with local names. They run with the compiler's own resources (files, stdin/stdout), so a macro that reads files, env or the clock is an input the pinned artifact silently depends on. Two majors of syn can coexist in one graph, and each is compiled separately. The 2025 compiler-performance survey post says derive expansion was not cached at the time (work underway), so every rebuild of a crate re-runs its derives. Raising build-override opt-level speeds expansion but slows the macro crates' own compile, and overrides cannot set panic, lto or rpath. A derive's check is only as strong as the macro: derive(Pod) reports a missing repr(C) as a plain error with no code and padding as E0080.
recipes.engine_note: The solver's own code uses no proc macro, yet every clean wasm build compiles four proc-macro crates from solver/Cargo.lock: nalgebra-macros, num-derive and profiling-procmacros on syn 2.0.119, thiserror-impl on syn 3.0.6. serde_derive 1.0.229 in the same lockfile also depends on syn 3.0.6, so a serde derive for world files would not add a third syn. If the stride-17 buffer is ever redesigned, a `#[derive(Pod)] #[repr(C)] struct Body` is the typed alternative to hand indices, proven padding-free at compile time.
recipes.verify_note: All 3 checks reproduced exactly against real bytemuck 1.25.2 (padding E0080, no-repr rejection, 17-f64 cast). Cargo.lock confirmed syn 2.0.119 vs 3.0.6 split exactly as claimed across the named crates.

recipes.name: Emit cargo:: lines from build.rs, pair rustc-cfg with rustc-check-cfg, and read the target from CARGO_CFG_*
recipes.what: A build script is a host program Cargo compiles and runs before the crate; since Cargo 1.77 it speaks `cargo::KEY=VALUE`, it must learn the target from CARGO_CFG_* (cfg! there describes the host), write only into OUT_DIR, and declare every cfg it sets.
recipes.how: Directives (Cargo Book): `cargo::rerun-if-changed=PATH` (a directory is scanned whole), `rerun-if-env-changed=VAR`, `rustc-cfg=KEY[="VALUE"]`, `rustc-check-cfg=CHECK_CFG` (respected from 1.80), `rustc-env=VAR=VALUE`, `warning=MSG`, `error=MSG` (1.84+, fails the build), `metadata=KEY=VALUE`, and the rustc-link-* family. `cargo::KEY=VALUE` needs Cargo 1.77 (rust-lang/cargo#12201, milestone 1.77.0); older toolchains need `cargo:KEY=VALUE`, where unsupported keys are taken as metadata. Measured on a scratch crate with `cargo +1.98.1 build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --offline`: `cargo::rustc-cfgg=x` -> error 'invalid output in build script ... Unknown key: `rustc-cfgg`', while `cargo:rustc-cfgg=x` passed silently; the script printed `cfg!(target_arch = "wasm32") = false` beside `CARGO_CFG_TARGET_ARCH = wasm32`, `CARGO_CFG_TARGET_FAMILY = wasm`, `HOST = x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`; with `rerun-if-changed=build.rs` and `=abi.txt`, editing src/lib.rs recompiled only the lib and editing abi.txt re-ran build-script-build; `cargo build -v` showed the script's lines arriving as `--cfg si_abi_generated --check-cfg 'cfg(si_abi_generated)'` next to Cargo's defaults `--check-cfg 'cfg(docsrs,test)' --check-cfg 'cfg(feature, values())'`. Generated code goes to `OUT_DIR` and in with `include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/abi.rs"));`. Cost, cold on this rig: a trivial script took 0.32 s to compile and 0.05 s to run against 0.13 s for the lib; the solver's graph compiles 8 dependency build scripts (0.34-0.49 s each) and runs them (0.08-0.29 s).
recipes.gotchas: `cargo::rustc-cfg=X` without `cargo::rustc-check-cfg=cfg(X)` makes every `#[cfg(X)]` warn unexpected_cfgs although X is set (measured). cfg!/#[cfg] inside build.rs test the host, so a wasm cross-build silently takes the host branch; the Cargo Book says to use CARGO_CFG_* instead. With no rerun-if line Cargo reruns the script whenever any file in the package changes. OUT_DIR is not cleaned between builds and may hold stale files. 'Scripts should not modify any files outside of that directory', so a build.rs cannot legitimately write a JS module next to the wasm. A build script is arbitrary host code inside the build: reading the clock, undeclared env vars or files outside the package makes the artifact depend on the machine.
recipes.engine_note: The solver has no build.rs; its generator is node (solver/build.mjs), outside Cargo. A build.rs that generated the ABI table could write only the Rust half into OUT_DIR, so build.mjs would still have to read the same data file itself; that is why the macro table in 'Pin the solver ABI with const _ assertions...' is the smaller change. If one is ever added, it must test CARGO_CFG_TARGET_FAMILY (wasm), never cfg! (the Linux or Windows host), and every clean build gains a compile and a run unit.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced live: cargo::rustc-cfgg=x fails with the exact Unknown key: rustc-cfgg text; cargo:rustc-cfgg=x passes silently; -v showed the claimed --cfg/--check-cfg lines verbatim; build script's cfg!/CARGO_CFG_* prints matched exactly.

recipes.name: Gate wasm code on target_family = "wasm" and turn a forbidden target feature into compile_error!
recipes.what: #[cfg] removes items before type checking, cfg! only yields a bool, and cfg_attr adds attributes conditionally; on 1.98.1 wasm32-unknown-unknown sets target_family = "wasm", target_arch = "wasm32", target_os = "unknown" and panic = "abort", so `#[cfg(target_feature = "relaxed-simd")] compile_error!(...)` turns a flag slip into a failed build.
recipes.how: `#[cfg(pred)]` on items with `all()`, `any()`, `not()`; `cfg!(pred)` is the literal true or false, so both branches must compile (calling a cfg'd-out fn is E0425); `#[cfg_attr(pred, a, b)]` expands to each listed attribute (the check exports `law_version` through `cfg_attr(target_family = "wasm", unsafe(no_mangle), inline(never))`). Measured `rustc +1.98.1 --print cfg`: wasm32-unknown-unknown -> target_family="wasm", target_arch="wasm32", target_os="unknown", panic="abort", target_feature bulk-memory, multivalue, mutable-globals, nontrapping-fptoint, reference-types, sign-ext; wasm32v1-none -> target_os="none" with only mutable-globals; `-C target-feature=+relaxed-simd` also sets simd128; `-C target-cpu=bleeding-edge` turns on relaxed-simd and simd128. The guard `#[cfg(target_feature = "relaxed-simd")] compile_error!("...");` compiles by default and fails with its message under +relaxed-simd. Name checking: Cargo 1.80+ passes --check-cfg by default and the warn-by-default unexpected_cfgs lint flags unknown names and values (measured: `#[cfg(si_abi_generatd)]` -> 'there is a config with a similar name: `si_abi_generated`'); declare static custom cfgs with `[lints.rust] unexpected_cfgs = { level = "warn", check-cfg = ['cfg(name)'] }` and build-script ones with `cargo::rustc-check-cfg`. Use target_family = "wasm" for any wasm target and target_arch = "wasm32" when the 32-bit pointer width matters.
recipes.rust_version: any; unexpected_cfgs on by default in Cargo 1.80+
recipes.gotchas: cfg! does not remove code; the other branch must still resolve and type-check. target_family can hold several values at once (the Reference names unix together with wasm), so compare, never assume a single value. Plain rustc, and this KB's oracle, checks cfg names only when a --check-cfg flag is passed ('Well known names and values are implicitly added as long as at least one --check-cfg argument is present'), so typos surface only in Cargo builds. A guard written as `#[cfg(not(target_family = "wasm"))] compile_error!` would also break host `cargo test` of pure functions: forbid the feature, not the host. The rustc feature name is relaxed-simd, and enabling it implies simd128.
recipes.engine_note: solver/.cargo/config.toml and solver/build.mjs both pass `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd` because RUSTFLAGS replaces the config's rustflags (build.mjs says so). Two lines in lib.rs, `#[cfg(target_feature = "relaxed-simd")] compile_error!(...)`, make the source refuse that configuration however the flags arrive, e.g. a `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=bleeding-edge"` build that forgot the disable. T3's opcode lint stays the check on the bytes. Measured on a scratch copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9: appended to the end of lib.rs, the guard left si_solver.wasm byte-identical, and a RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=bleeding-edge' build then failed with the guard's message.
recipes.verify_note: rustc --print cfg for all 4 target/flag combos matches exactly. All 7 checks reproduced (cfg_word=23/31/19, compile_error! trigger, E0425, cfg_attr). wasm_no_imports holds (0 imports). config.toml+build.mjs both pass the flag.

recipes.name: Compute tables in const fn with while, match and &mut; expect E0015 on for-loops, trait calls and formatting
recipes.what: On 1.98.1 const code runs loop/while/if/match, takes &mut (1.83), does float arithmetic (1.82) and panics with literal messages (1.57); for-loops, iterator methods, trait operators on your own types, PartialEq on str, heap allocation and formatted panic messages are refused.
recipes.how: Const contexts, always evaluated at compile time: array lengths and repeat counts, const and static initializers, enum discriminants, const generic arguments, `const { }` blocks. Write loops as `let mut i = 0; while i < N { ...; i += 1; }` or `loop { ... break v; }`; pass `&mut [T; N]` into a const fn to fill a table in place and bind the result: `const TABLE: [f64; 4] = { let mut t = [0.0; 4]; fill(&mut t, 0.25); t };`. Panic with `panic!("literal")` or `assert!(cond, "literal")` (one &str through `{}` also works); failure is E0080 'evaluation panicked: ...'. Measured refusals on 1.98.1: `for i in 0..n` -> E0015 'cannot use `for` loop on `std::ops::Range<u32>` in constant functions'; `a.iter().sum()` -> E0015 plus '`iter` is not yet stable as a const fn'; `a + b` through a user `impl Add` -> E0015 'cannot call non-const operator'; `a == b` on &str -> E0658 '`PartialEq` is not yet stable as a const trait'; `Vec::push` -> E0658 plus E0493 (destructor at compile time); `assert!(x == 17, "stride is {}", x)` with a usize -> E0015 'cannot call non-const formatting macro'.
recipes.rust_version: 1.83+ (&mut in const), 1.82+ (float ops in const fn), 1.57+ (panic in const); no stable const traits on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: A const fn called outside a const context is not guaranteed to run at compile time; bind it to a const or wrap it in `const { }` to force it. Overflow and out-of-bounds indexing in a const context are compile errors, not wraps or run-time panics. A mutable reference may not become part of a const's final value (1.83 post). Generic code over `T: Add` cannot be const on stable, so write concrete f64/usize const fns.
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs's `step` and `resolve_pair` already use index while loops, a const-compatible style. The realistic const work in the solver is proofs and tables over the ABI constants (see 'Pin the solver ABI with const _ assertions...'); the step itself reads `static mut` buffers at run time and stays an ordinary fn.
recipes.verify_note: All 8 checks reproduced exactly: main demo matches; for/iterator/operator/format-macro in const fn are E0015; str== is E0658; Vec::push is E0658+E0493; a reached panic is E0080. resolve_pair/step use a const-compatible while-loop style.

recipes.name: Trust const f64 bits for + - * /, but keep d * PI / 180.0: to_radians() differs on 93 of 361 integer degrees
recipes.what: rustc evaluates const float arithmetic in the soft-float rustc_apfloat, so finite + - * / results are the IEEE bits an IEEE-conforming target computes at run time, whatever the build host (only NaN sign and payload may differ); sqrt, powi, exp, sin and cos are not const on 1.98.1; and to_radians() multiplies by a pre-rounded PI / 180, a different rounding from d * PI / 180.0.
recipes.how: Float operations in const fn are stable since 1.82; RFC 3514 fixes + - * / % and sqrt to IEEE 754 results with non-deterministic NaN sign and payload, which may differ between compile time and run time. At tag 1.98.1, rustc_const_eval/src/interpret/operator.rs computes float Add/Sub/Mul/Div/Rem as `(l op r).value` on rustc_apfloat types followed by `adjust_nan`; rustc_apfloat is a Rust port of LLVM's APFloat softfloat with no host floating-point use. Measured under 1.98.1: `50.0 * PI / 180.0` as a const, at run time behind black_box, and as `50f64.to_radians()` are all 0x3febecde5da115a9; `FRAC_PI_4` and `45.0 * PI / 180.0` are both 0x3fe921fb54442d18; a wasm32 export computing `d * PI / 180.0` under node v22 matched the compiler's consts bit for bit for d = 50, 45 and 46. But `46.0 * PI / 180.0` = 0x3fe9b0f58956c201 while `46f64.to_radians()` = 0x3fe9b0f58956c202, because core computes `self * RADS_PER_DEG` with `RADS_PER_DEG = PI / 180.0`. Over integer degrees 0..=360, JS `d * Math.PI / 180` equals Rust `d * PI / 180.0` for 361 of 361 and `d.to_radians()` for 268; the other 93 differ by exactly one ulp. Const-callable on 1.98.1 (compiler): abs, signum, copysign, min, max, clamp, recip, to_degrees, to_radians, floor, ceil, round, round_ties_even, trunc, fract, mul_add, midpoint, to_bits, from_bits; not const: sqrt, powi, exp, sin, cos, rem_euclid (E0015) and total_cmp (not yet const-stable). NaN: on this x86_64 host `0.0 / 0.0` is 0x7ff8000000000000 (positive) as a const and 0xfff8000000000000 (negative) at run time, the 1.82 post's own example.
recipes.rust_version: 1.82+ (float ops in const fn); to_radians and to_degrees const since 1.85
recipes.gotchas: Do not tidy `50.0 * PI / 180.0` into `50f64.to_radians()` without comparing bits: equal for 44, 45 and 50, one ulp apart for 3, 46, 51 and 90 other integer degrees. Transcendentals have unspecified precision at run time and are not const, so a compile-time sin/cos table needs a pinned offline generator and literal bits. Never compare or hash a NaN made in const against one made at run time. core's comment calls PI / 180 'correctly rounded with respect to the true value', which is still a different rounding path from the (d * PI) / 180 order that JS uses.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs: CLIMB_ANGLE = FRAC_PI_4 (0x3fe921fb54442d18) and SLIDE_ANGLE = 50.0 * PI / 180.0 (0x3febecde5da115a9) are produced by the compiler's soft-float, independent of the build host, and equal to what V8 computes at run time in wasm from the same expression. For T4's 44 deg / 46 deg climb course, build angles as `d * PI / 180.0` in Rust and `d * Math.PI / 180` in JS: `46f64.to_radians()` is one ulp away from both.
recipes.verify_note: Independently reproduced: 93/361 degrees differ by 1 ulp between d*PI/180.0 and to_radians(); every claimed hex bit pattern (50/45/46/3 deg, NaN sign, wasm/node) matched exactly; sin/sqrt non-const. rapier_law.rs constants verbatim.

recipes.name: Use const for values, static for one address, const { } for non-Copy repeats and generic compile-time asserts
recipes.what: A const is inlined as a fresh value at every use, so interior mutability on it does nothing (rustc warns), while a static has one address and must be Sync unless mut; inline `const { }` blocks (1.79) run at compile time inside functions, may use generics, and fail per instantiation.
recipes.how: Reference rule: prefer const unless you store a lot of data, need the single-address property, or need interior mutability. Measured: `const COUNTER: AtomicU32` plus two fetch_add still loads 0 and rustc warns `const_item_interior_mutations`; the same `static` loads 2 and two `&raw const` of it compare equal; `static FLAG: Cell<bool>` is E0277 (not Sync). `[const { Vec::new() }; 4]` builds an array of a non-Copy type where `[Vec::new(); 4]` is E0277 (Copy). `fn stride_of<const N: usize>()` with `const { assert!(N > 0, "...") }` compiles for 17 and stops a binary's build for 0 with E0080 '... while instantiating `fn stride_of::<0>`'; the same `assert!` outside `const { }` compiles and panics at run time (exit 101).
recipes.gotchas: A const holding a Vec, Cell, atomic or Once gives each use a fresh copy; state belongs in a static. A const block that is never executed 'may or may not be evaluated' (Reference): the same stride_of file compiled as a lib, where main is unused and nothing instantiates stride_of::<0>, built cleanly on 1.98.1, so a generic const assertion guards only instantiations that are actually codegen'd. Large tables in a const are copied into each use site. static mut needs unsafe and its references are an unsafe-ffi topic (static_mut_refs). The 1.79 stabilization is for const blocks in expression position.
recipes.engine_note: BODIES, COLLIDERS and HEIGHTS must stay statics: bodies_ptr(), colliders_ptr() and heights_ptr() hand JS one address that its Float64Array views index. Their lengths (MAX_BODIES * BODY_STRIDE, MAX_COLLIDERS * COLLIDER_STRIDE, MAX_HEIGHTS) and the SOLVER initializer (`Solver { loaded: None, snapshot: Vec::new() }`) are const contexts. DT, G, the strides and the angles are rightly consts.
recipes.verify_note: All 7 checks reproduced: const_item_interior_mutations fires w/ exact stdout, static Cell is E0277, inline-const-vs-Copy is E0277, generic const-assert is E0080 only on the bad instantiation. SOLVER static init confirmed in rapier_law.rs.

recipes.name: Keep const generics to standalone integer, bool and char params; size nested arrays, never N * STRIDE
recipes.what: Stable const generics (since 1.51) take integer, bool and char parameters used standalone in types; arithmetic on a parameter inside a type, f64 or &str parameters, and #![feature(generic_const_exprs)] are all refused on 1.98.1.
recipes.how: Write `struct Pool<const N: usize, const STRIDE: usize> { data: [[f64; STRIDE]; N] }` and flatten with `as_flattened()` (stable 1.80; `[[f64; 17]; 2]` -> 34 contiguous f64, 272 bytes). Derived numbers go in associated consts (`const WORDS: usize = N * STRIDE;`) or `const { }` blocks, usable in expressions but not in types (`[f64; Self::WORDS]` -> 'generic `Self` types are currently not permitted in anonymous constants'). A const argument must be a literal, a single identifier or a braced block: `f::<{ K + 1 }>()` with K a const item compiles; `[f64; N * 17]` with N a parameter -> 'generic parameters may not be used in const operations'. Parameter types are u8..u128, usize, i8..i128, isize, char and bool; `const RAD: f64` -> '`f64` is forbidden as the type of a const generic parameter'; `#![feature(generic_const_exprs)]` (tracking issue #76560) -> E0554 on stable.
recipes.gotchas: Every distinct <N, STRIDE> is a separate monomorphized copy. rustc itself marks generic_const_exprs incomplete ('may not be safe to use and/or cause compiler crashes', printed with the E0554 error). An angle or tolerance cannot be a const parameter; keep it a const item. In a type a parameter must stand alone ({N} is accepted, {N + 1} is not).
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs's `[f64; MAX_BODIES * BODY_STRIDE]` compiles because MAX_BODIES and BODY_STRIDE are const items, not generic parameters. Making the body count generic would force `[[f64; BODY_STRIDE]; N]` (the same 64 x 136 bytes, flattened with as_flattened) and buys nothing while the ABI is fixed at 64 x 17.
recipes.verify_note: All 6 checks reproduced exactly: verbatim stderr for 3 messages (generic params in const ops / generic Self types / f64 forbidden) and E0554+incomplete_features. lib.rs confirmed MAX_BODIES*BODY_STRIDE uses const items, not generics.

recipes.name: Pin the solver ABI with const _ assertions and generate the JS strides from one Rust table, not by hand
recipes.what: `const _: () = { ... }` blocks, offset_of! (1.77) and size_of turn layout and slot invariants into E0080 build failures that add no bytes when appended; a macro_rules! table can emit the consts, the proof and one exported descriptor so JS never retypes 17 or 10.
recipes.how: Free const items are always evaluated, even inside unused functions, so the proof runs on every build. Proof: list every slot of the record, `const SLOTS: [usize; BODY_STRIDE] = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, QX, QY, QZ, QW, WX, WY, WZ, HX, HY, HZ, DRIVEN];`, then check in while loops that each is below BODY_STRIDE and no two are equal: 17 distinct values below 17 cover the record exactly once. Mirror the layout in a `#[repr(C)]` struct and assert `size_of::<Body>() == BODY_STRIDE * 8` and `offset_of!(Body, driven) == DRIVEN * 8`. A macro `abi_layout! { BODY_STRIDE = 17; HX = 13, HY = 14, HZ = 15, DRIVEN = 16 }` emits the consts, the same proof and `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C" fn abi_word(i: u32) -> u32` over a static table; the check builds it for wasm32 and abi_word(0) returns 17. Measured bytes. In a test cdylib (rustc 1.98.1, wasm32-unknown-unknown, opt-level 3, panic=abort, codegen-units 1, strip=debuginfo, same file and output names) appending a const-assert block, or a cfg-guarded compile_error!, after the last line left the .wasm SHA-256 unchanged, while inserting one line, assertion or comment, above an indexing expression changed exactly one byte of the data section: the panic Location line went from 10 to 11. On a scratch copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9 (`cargo +1.98.1 build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --offline --locked`, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd', Windows host): appending the 17-slot proof to rapier_law.rs and the relaxed-simd guard to lib.rs kept si_solver.wasm at SHA-256 c8782b06d03c046a...; one comment line inserted at the top of rapier_law.rs changed it to b308cfd2e80bf850..., the same line at the top of lib.rs did not.
recipes.gotchas: Messages in const assertions must be literals or one &str through {}; formatting a usize is E0015. offset_of! on a repr(Rust) type may change between compilations, so assert offsets only on repr(C). A const _ proof guards the Rust side only; build.mjs's literals can still drift until the glue reads the numbers from the module or from a generated file. Any edit that shifts lines above a panic site that survives optimization, even a comment, changes the wasm bytes and the pinned digest (measured on the solver: one line added at the top of rapier_law.rs changed the digest, at the top of lib.rs it did not, presumably because no lib.rs panic location survives optimization): append new proofs at the end of a file, or take one deliberate digest bump. The output file name also has to match when comparing bytes: two builds of one source differed only by `-o` name in this measurement.
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs declares BODY_STRIDE = 17, HX = 13, HY = 14, HZ = 15, DRIVEN = 16, COLLIDER_STRIDE = 10 and rapier_law.rs QX = 6 .. WZ = 12 (slots 0-5 are bare literals), while the module build.mjs generates hard-codes `i * 17` four times, `j * 10` twice and `view[at + 13..16]` eight times (e5fbcb9). Step one costs no bytes, measured: the 17-slot SLOTS proof appended to the end of rapier_law.rs, which already sees both sets of constants, compiled under the crate's edition 2021 and left si_solver.wasm unchanged. Step two removes the JS copy: build.mjs reads abi_word(i) from the module it has just built and emits the offsets; that export is new code, so the digest pin moves once, in the same commit.
recipes.verify_note: All 5 checks reproduced exactly (17-slot proof, slot-collision E0080, macro->wasm abi_word(0)=17, macro-proof-fail E0080, unused-generic E0080). engine_note's count is wrong: build.mjs shows the write-block twice on main, not eight.

corrections.claim: engine_note says build.mjs hard-codes view[at + 13..16] eight times. Grep on main (2026-09-25) shows this HX/HY/HZ write-block occurs exactly twice (stepBodies + writeInputs = 6 individual lines), not eight. i*17 (four) and j*10 (twice) are correct as stated.

recipes.name: Embed build inputs with include_bytes!, include_str!, env! and concat!, and know which of them fail the build
recipes.what: include_bytes!/include_str! embed a file located relative to the current source file, env! bakes in a compile-time variable and fails the build when it is unset (option_env! returns None), concat! joins literals into a &'static str, stringify! returns tokens as text, and compile_error! stops the build with your message.
recipes.how: `include_bytes!("pinned/si_solver.wasm")` -> `&'static [u8; N]`, the path relative to the current file and interpreted per platform (write `/`); a missing file fails with 'couldn't read ...'. `env!("NAME")` -> `&'static str`; unset -> 'environment variable `NAME` not defined at compile time'; `env!("NAME", "msg")` replaces the text; `option_env!("NAME")` -> `Option<&'static str>`. `concat!("si-solver/", 17, "/", 2.5, "/", true, "/", 'x')` -> "si-solver/17/2.5/true/x"; arguments may be macro calls that expand to literals (stringify!, env!, your own). `stringify!(BODY_STRIDE * 8 + HX)` -> "BODY_STRIDE * 8 + HX". They compose with const fn: a const FNV-1a over `include_bytes!(file!())` is computed during compilation and equals a run-time recomputation. `compile_error!` in a macro_rules! fallback arm turns bad input into your message (`law!(havok)` -> 'law! accepts `box` or `rapier`').
recipes.gotchas: env! reads the environment of the rustc process, so a variable present on one CI machine and absent on another changes the bytes or breaks the build; under Cargo, OUT_DIR is set only during compilation. std warns that stringify!'s expansion 'may change in the future': use it for single identifiers in a names table, never as hashed or persisted text. A backslash path in include_bytes! does not compile on Unix. include_bytes! copies the file into the artifact at compile time; a changed file means a rebuild, not a reload.
recipes.engine_note: build.mjs embeds the pinned wasm into JS as a Uint8Array literal. A native Rust host shell (the Godot or Unreal bindings slice) would embed it with include_bytes!(".../si_solver.wasm") and can refuse to compile against any other module with a const-fn digest check over those bytes; the pin itself stays the SHA-256 in fixtures/solver.sha256, and FNV-1a here only demonstrates compile-time hashing.
recipes.verify_note: All 6 checks reproduced: verbatim env! unset/custom-message text, include_bytes! couldn't-read text, compile_error! fallback text, const FNV-1a over include_bytes!(file!()) matches run time. build.mjs embeds wasm as a Uint8Array literal.

lanes.title: Memory, smart pointers & layout
lanes.verifier_note: Retrieved all 58 warrant sources across the 10 recipes directly (WebFetch against doc.rust-lang.org/stable at pinned 1.98.1, docs.rs at the pinned crate versions rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 / parry3d-f64 0.30.2 / slotmap 1.1.1 / typed-arena 2.0.2 / bumpalo 3.20.3); read solver/src/lib.rs, solver/src/rapier_law.rs, solver/build.mjs and solver/Cargo.toml from si-rpg-engine at main via read-only gh api for every engine_note; and additionally ran all 29 embedded checks myself through this lane's own scripts/compile_oracle.py against the actual pinned rustc 1.98.1 (already installed and set up locally) rather than relying only on the operator's separate run -- 29/29 passed with exact stdout, error-code, lint and wasm_call matches, including the wasm32 alignment probe (800) and every 'measured' byte-size claim (repr(Rust) reorder=8, Option<RigidBodyHandle>=12, Option<DefaultKey>=8, Plain=8/Tagged=16). Every source supported its claim as stated and every engine_note fact matched the live repository precisely, several down to exact line-level code (the ContactPair ptr::from_ref/&mut* cast, build_world's collider-then-heightfield-then-body insertion order, build.mjs's bodies_ptr()/8+i*17+slot indexing, snapshot_ptr/len read-then-copy ordering). The one systemic weakness: 2 of 10 recipes (mutate-through-unsafecell, re-read-a-vec-pointer) each have one check whose own label claims code 'compiles silently' / 'with no diagnostic at all', but neither check sets the schema's `no_warnings` field, so compile_oracle's pass/fail gate only verifies returncode 0, not silence -- a future stray lint would still show PASS. I independently compiled both and confirmed stderr is genuinely empty today (claims hold), but the checks as written don't enforce their own strongest claim; no recipe in this lane uses `no_warnings` at all despite the field existing for exactly this purpose.

recipes.name: Put ABI buffers in flat arrays or #[repr(C)]: default repr(Rust) promises no field order or size
recipes.what: Rust fixes the layout of arrays (element n at byte n*size_of::<T>()), of #[repr(C)] types (declaration order, C padding) and of #[repr(transparent)] types (the layout and ABI of their one non-zero-sized field); the default representation promises only aligned, non-overlapping fields, and its order and size may differ between compilations.
recipes.how: For memory another language reads (JS Float64Array views over wasm memory, a snapshot byte format, a C header) use a flat [f64; N] addressed by stride constants, or a #[repr(C)] struct of primitives. Pin the layout at compile time with `const _: () = assert!(size_of::<T>() == N);` (size_of is a const fn) and `core::mem::offset_of!(T, field)` (stable since 1.77). Order repr(C) fields by descending alignment to avoid padding: #[repr(C)] { u8, u32, u16 } is 12 bytes at offsets 0/4/8. To read a field of a #[repr(packed)] struct, copy it (`{ w.value }`) or take `&raw const w.value` and call read_unaligned(); a reference to it is refused with E0793.
recipes.gotchas: The repr(Rust) twin of { u8, u32, u16 } measures 8 bytes on rustc 1.98.1 because the compiler reordered it; that is an observation, and the Reference says the default representation makes no other layout guarantees. Primitive alignment is platform-specific (the Reference: f64 is only 4-aligned on many 32-bit platforms; u128 alignment varies), so measure on the shipped target: on wasm32-unknown-unknown align_of::<f64>() is 8. A reference to a packed field is a hard error (E0793) because a misaligned reference is undefined behaviour even if it is never dereferenced.
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs exposes `static mut BODIES: [f64; MAX_BODIES * BODY_STRIDE]` (64 x 17) and COLLIDERS (64 x 10), rapier_law.rs HEIGHTS ([f64; 256]); build.mjs indexes a Float64Array at `bodies_ptr() / 8 + i * 17 + slot`. That is the guaranteed case: array element n sits at n*8 bytes, and the wasm check below returns 800 (f64 8-aligned, the static's address a multiple of 8). Keep the ABI as flat arrays or #[repr(C)]; a plain `struct Body { .. }` would give JS no fixed offsets. The coupling no compiler checks is the stride: build.mjs hard-codes 17 and 10 while Rust owns BODY_STRIDE and COLLIDER_STRIDE, so exporting the strides or generating the JS constants would turn a stride change into a loud failure.

recipes.name: Count on Option's niche only for std-listed types; give boundary enums #[repr(u8)] and explicit values
recipes.what: Option<T> has exactly the size, alignment and call ABI of T when T is &U, &mut U, Box<U>, a fn pointer, a NonZero integer, NonNull<U>, or a #[repr(transparent)] wrapper of one of these; types in which every bit pattern is valid (u32, f64) have no niche, so Option<u32> is 8 bytes and Option<f64> is 16.
recipes.how: Use NonZeroU32 (NonZero<u32>) for ids that are never 0, and Option<&T> / Option<Box<T>> instead of nullable raw pointers: all free under the guarantee. Give a fieldless enum that crosses a boundary #[repr(u8)] and explicit discriminants; the Reference makes it the size of u8 with discriminants 0..=255, and a value of 300 is rejected by the deny-by-default overflowing_literals lint. Decode incoming numbers with match or a TryFrom impl that returns Err for anything else.
recipes.gotchas: Niche filling outside the std list is the compiler's choice, not a promise: slotmap's key is a repr(Rust) struct { idx: u32, version: NonZeroU32 } and Option<DefaultKey> measures 8 bytes on 1.98.1, but std guarantees that only for the listed types. An explicit repr on an enum WITH fields turns niche filling off: enum { Nothing, Some(&u16) } is 8 bytes plain and 16 bytes with #[repr(u8)] (Rustonomicon; measured). Option<MaybeUninit<bool>> is 2 bytes because MaybeUninit has no invalid values.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs keeps `handles: Vec<Option<RigidBodyHandle>>`; RigidBodyHandle is #[repr(transparent)] over rapier's Index { index: u32, generation: u32 }, which has no invalid bit pattern, so each slot costs 12 bytes (measured), harmless at 64 bodies. The body mode travels as the f64 in slot DRIVEN (16) and is tested with == 1.0 / 2.0 / 3.0; if it becomes a Rust enum, #[repr(u8)] plus a TryFrom<f64> keeps a stray 7.0 from JS an error instead of an invalid value.

recipes.name: Budget pointer widths: Box<T> is one word, Box<[T]> and &dyn Trait carry metadata, ZSTs take no space
recipes.what: Box<T> for sized T is guaranteed to be one pointer, ABI-compatible with C's T*; pointers to dynamically sized types ([T], str, dyn Trait) also carry a length or a vtable pointer and are two words today; zero-sized types occupy no memory, and a Vec of a ZST never allocates and reports capacity usize::MAX.
recipes.how: Keep fixed-size data inline, on the stack or in a static; the Book: stack data must have a known, fixed size, while data whose size is unknown at compile time or can change goes on the heap. Box::new moves a value to the heap. vec.into_boxed_slice() discards excess capacity and yields a Box<[T]>: a fixed-length heap buffer with no capacity field, so it cannot grow and its allocation stays put for the box's life. Vec<T> is a (pointer, capacity, length) triplet (field order unspecified) that never stores elements inline on the stack. Use unit structs and PhantomData as markers and Map<K, ()> as a set: stores of a ZST compile to nothing.
recipes.gotchas: The Reference hedges on DST pointer width: all pointers to DSTs are 'currently' twice the size of usize, 'though you should not rely on this'; assert it in a const only for the target you ship. Unsafe code must special-case ZSTs: pointer offsets are no-ops and allocators require a non-zero size (Rustonomicon), and a Box of a ZST holds a dangling but aligned pointer.
recipes.engine_note: The ABI buffers (BODIES and COLLIDERS in lib.rs, HEIGHTS in rapier_law.rs) are statics, neither stack nor heap: all references and raw pointers to a static refer to the same allocation, so their addresses never change. The heap holds the Rapier world, SOLVER.snapshot and the per-quantum scratch Vecs in integrate(). If an ABI buffer ever needs a length chosen at load time, a Box<[f64]> made once with into_boxed_slice keeps the fixed address that a growing Vec lacks.

recipes.name: Predict destructors: fields drop in declaration order, locals in reverse, statics and forgotten values never
recipes.what: A struct's fields drop in declaration order and a scope's locals in reverse order of declaration; an assignment drops the old value before the new one moves in; statics are never dropped; mem::forget and ManuallyDrop skip a destructor safely, because Rust does not promise that destructors run; memory that is not yet initialised must be held as MaybeUninit<T>.
recipes.how: Get the drop order you need by ordering fields: ManuallyDrop's docs recommend reordering declarations over ManuallyDrop, which needs unsafe code to drop. Use ManuallyDrop<T> (same layout and bit validity as T) when ownership passes to foreign code, in preference to mem::forget. To fill an array piecewise: `let mut a: [MaybeUninit<T>; N] = [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N];`, write every slot exactly once, then `mem::transmute::<_, [T; N]>(a)`; MaybeUninit<T> has T's size, alignment and ABI.
recipes.gotchas: `MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init()` for bool (or any type with invalid bit patterns) is undefined behaviour, and rustc 1.98.1 only warns, through the warn-by-default invalid_value lint ('does not permit being left uninitialized'), so deny warnings in CI. Dropping a MaybeUninit does nothing: a panic midway through a fill leaks, it never double-drops. Calling ManuallyDrop::drop twice is UB. Rc cycles and process::exit also skip destructors, so no soundness argument may rest on Drop running.
recipes.engine_note: `static mut SOLVER` in rapier_law.rs is a static, so it is never dropped: its snapshot buffer and loaded Rapier world live as long as the wasm instance. The one release point is replacement: `solver.loaded = Some(loaded)` in ensure() drops the previous Loaded (fields in declaration order, the PhysicsWorld first) before the new one moves in. A T2 solver_restore that rebuilds the world inherits that same drop point.

recipes.name: Point Rc/Arc edges one way (strong down, Weak back) or a strong cycle leaks and its destructors never run
recipes.what: Rc and Arc drop their value when the last strong handle goes, so a cycle of strong handles never reaches zero: no destructor runs and nothing warns, because leaks are memory-safe in Rust. Weak (Rc::downgrade / Arc::downgrade) does not own, and upgrade() returns None once the value is gone.
recipes.how: Shape shared ownership as a tree: parent to child as Rc/Arc, child to parent as Weak, upgrade() at the point of use. Rc's count is non-atomic and Rc is not Send (moving one into thread::spawn is E0277); Arc's count is atomic and Arc<T> is Send + Sync as long as T is, because Arc makes shared ownership thread-safe but adds no thread safety to the data, so mutation behind it needs Mutex, RwLock or atomics. Write Rc::clone(&x) / Arc::clone(&x) to show a count bump rather than a deep copy. For simulation state prefer a single owner (a Vec or an arena) plus Copy indices, and keep Rc/Arc for immutable shared leaves such as collision shapes.
recipes.gotchas: A leaked cycle is silent: in the check, strong_count stays 1 and no drop line prints after both handles are dropped. Clone shares, rebuilding does not: constructing the same shape twice makes two allocations (Arc::ptr_eq is false). Preferring arenas over Rc graphs for simulation state is this lane's inference (no cycles, state addressed by position), not a sentence from a source.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs builds a fresh parry SharedShape (`pub struct SharedShape(pub Arc<dyn Shape>)`) on every character_shape() call in integrate(): once per non-lifted driven body for move_shape and once per plan for the impulse pass, so each quantum makes one or two new Arc allocations per driven body. Building it once per body in build_world and keeping it in Loaded would make each later use a count bump (a clone shares the allocation, per the check). The shape's numbers are identical, so results should not move; confirm with the golden hash.

recipes.name: Mutate through & only via UnsafeCell-based types; a &T-to-&mut T cast is UB even where the lint is silent
recipes.what: UnsafeCell<T> is the only allowed way to mutate data behind a shared reference, and Cell, RefCell, OnceCell, LazyCell and the thread-safe cells and atomics are built on it; mutating through a &T any other way, including a &T -> *mut T -> &mut T cast, is undefined behaviour.
recipes.how: Pick by thread and write pattern: Cell<T> (values moved or copied in and out, no borrow tracking); RefCell<T> (borrows checked at run time: a second borrow_mut panics with 'RefCell already borrowed', try_borrow_mut returns Err instead); OnceCell<T> and LazyCell<T, F> (written once). For statics and threads use the Sync counterparts: Mutex / RwLock, OnceLock<T> (1.70) and LazyLock<T, F> (1.80; initialises on first access and is poisoned if the initialiser panics). A static must be Sync, so RefCell, LazyCell and bare UnsafeCell statics fail with E0277. When a library hands you only &T and you must write, get a &mut path from the owner or rebuild the data; never cast.
recipes.gotchas: The deny-by-default invalid_reference_casting lint rejects `&mut *(ptr::from_ref(x) as *mut T)` written as one expression ('casting `&T` to `&mut T` is undefined behavior, even if the reference is unused'), but it matches a pattern: the same cast with the pointer parked in a Vec<*mut T> and dereferenced later compiles with no diagnostic at all. UnsafeCell lifts only the immutability of shared references: there is no legal way to obtain aliasing &mut, even with UnsafeCell, and it does nothing against data races. RefCell turns a borrow bug into a run-time panic, not a compile error.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs solver_clear_warmstart() collects `core::ptr::from_ref(pair) as *mut ContactPair` for each &ContactPair that `narrow_phase.contact_pairs()` yields, then writes the manifold points through `&mut *ptr`. rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 offers no &mut path: every NarrowPhase accessor (contact_pairs, contact_pair, contact_graph) takes &self and returns shared references, and ContactPair's manifolds and solver_clusters are plain Vec<ContactManifold>, not cells. rustc denies this cast when it is written inline and accepts it once the pointer goes through a Vec (the first two checks), so the export compiles cleanly but sits outside what the std docs and the lint text permit. T2's solver_restore must write warm-start impulses into the same points: build it, and the clear, on a sound path (rebuild the world from the bytes, or a &mut accessor in a pinned rapier patch) rather than on this cast. What Miri's aliasing models say about it is the unsafe-ffi lane's question.

recipes.name: Return Cow when a function usually passes its input through and only sometimes rewrites it
recipes.what: Cow (clone-on-write) holds either borrowed data or its owned form; to_mut() clones only on the first write, so the common no-change path allocates nothing, which is the pattern std itself uses in String::from_utf8_lossy.
recipes.how: Start from Cow::Borrowed(input), call out.to_mut() at the first element that needs changing (it clones the whole slice once; later writes reuse the owned copy) and return the Cow; callers read through Deref or take ownership with into_owned(). Cow<'a, B> needs B: ToOwned + ?Sized, so it works for [T] (owned as Vec<T>) and str (owned as String).
recipes.gotchas: to_mut() on a borrowed Cow copies the whole slice even to change one element, so a function that nearly always writes should return Vec<T>. Only a match on Cow::Borrowed / Cow::Owned tells you which case you got; Deref hides it. A returned Cow borrows its input and cannot outlive it.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs canonicalises signed zero one value at a time (canon() inside push_f64 and write_body), which needs no Cow. The pattern fits a whole-buffer canonicalising or validating pass that usually finds nothing to change, like the check's signed-zero canonicaliser.
recipes.verify_note: Cow and from_utf8_lossy docs confirmed verbatim (clone-on-write, to_mut clones only if not owned, B:'a+ToOwned+?Sized). Engine_note's contrast with canon()'s one-value-at-a-time style is accurate. Oracle check passes with exact stdout.

recipes.name: Store indices or offsets instead of self-references; use Pin only where an API such as Future::poll needs it
recipes.what: A struct cannot safely hold a reference into its own fields, because moving it would leave the pointer at the old address, and the borrow checker refuses to build one (E0505, E0515). Pin guarantees that a !Unpin value stays at one address until it is dropped; most types are Unpin, and for them Pin adds nothing.
recipes.how: Replace a self-pointer with an index or byte offset into the owned buffer (`last: usize` into `samples: Vec<f64>`): it survives every move, clone and serialisation. Reach for Pin only when an API demands it (Future::poll takes `self: Pin<&mut Self>`) or when writing an address-sensitive type, which opts out of Unpin with a PhantomPinned field. Pin on the stack with std::pin::pin! (stable 1.68; no heap allocation, and the pin cannot escape its block) or on the heap with Box::pin.
recipes.gotchas: Pin::new accepts only Unpin targets; for a !Unpin value it fails with E0277 ('`PhantomPinned` cannot be unpinned'), and rustc suggests pin! or Box::pin. A pinned value's memory must stay valid until its drop runs, so it cannot be overwritten without dropping it first. Pin alone does not make a self-referential struct writable in safe code: the std::pin example keeps its self-pointer as a NonNull, a raw pointer.
recipes.engine_note: Nothing in the solver needs Pin: world state sits in `static mut SOLVER`, bodies are named by Rapier handles (indices), body records by position in BODIES, and the snapshot is a byte string. That is what lets T2's solver_restore rebuild a world from bytes: every cross-reference is an index that means the same thing after the rebuild, which a stored address would not.
recipes.verify_note: std::pin/pin!/Future::poll confirmed verbatim. Engine's index-based handles (Rapier handles, no self-refs, no Pin use anywhere in rapier_law.rs) match the claim. Oracle: 3/3 pass, incl. both E0505+E0515 together and E0277.

recipes.name: Keep entities in a generational arena keyed by (index, generation); insertion order hands out the ids
recipes.what: A generational arena (slotmap, Rapier's RigidBodySet and ColliderSet) stores values in a Vec and returns a Copy key of slot index plus version, so a removed key stays invalid even after its slot is reused; which index a value gets is decided by insertion order and the free list, and in Rapier the generation is one counter for the whole arena.
recipes.how: Give each kind of entity its own key type (slotmap's new_key_type!; a key used on the wrong map is safe but unspecified), store keys rather than references, and resolve with get(), which returns None for a stale key. Where state is hashed or restored, insert in a fixed order and sort by an explicit tuple such as Rapier's into_raw_parts() -> (index, generation). Use typed-arena when values of one type all live until the arena drops (allocation is typically a Vec push, and values may form cycles), and a bump allocator such as bumpalo for phase-oriented scratch freed all at once (its Drop impls are not run).
recipes.gotchas: slotmap keys implement Ord, but its docs say key order is unspecified and as_ffi() promises nothing about the value, so never order hashed output by slotmap key. In rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 every removal bumps one arena-wide generation and pushes the freed index onto a LIFO free list: after one removal the reused slot returns as (2, 1) and even a never-used slot starts at generation 1, so ids depend on removal history, not only on what exists. slotmap versions can wrap after 2^31 reuses of one slot.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs build_world inserts the fixed colliders first, then the heightfield, then each non-carried body, so a record index i is not its RigidBodyHandle index; hence `handles: Vec<Option<RigidBodyHandle>>`. rebuild_snapshot sorts contact pairs by `(collider1.into_raw_parts(), collider2.into_raw_parts())` and writes each index and generation into the hashed bytes, so the hash depends on insertion order (the subject of T3's insertion-order test) and on generations. Today every world is built fresh and nothing is removed, so every generation is 0; once any path removes a body or collider, the generations of everything inserted later shift, and T2's rebuild from bytes would reproduce the snapshot only by replaying the same removals.
recipes.verify_note: slotmap docs+source and rapier arena.rs source confirmed field-for-field (Index{index,generation}, arena-wide generation, LIFO free list). build_world order matches exactly. Oracle: 2/2 pass.
