recipes.name: Re-read a Vec's pointer after any call that can grow it: growth reallocates and kills raw pointers into it
recipes.what: A Vec (re)allocates when a push finds len == capacity, and after a successful realloc any access through the old pointer is undefined behaviour even if the block stayed in place; within capacity push never reallocates, clear() keeps the buffer, and Vec::new() allocates nothing until the first push.
recipes.how: Hand out a buffer's pointer and length from calls made after the last mutation (read ptr, then len, then copy) and never cache them across calls. Size up front (Vec::with_capacity(n) requests exactly n elements) and reuse with clear() so steady-state steps never touch the allocator. Where the borrow checker can see it, a &v[i] held across v.push is refused (E0502); raw pointers get no such check. To observe allocation, register a counting #[global_allocator]: a static whose type implements GlobalAlloc, allowed once per crate graph (cdylib and staticlib otherwise use System). It must not unwind, and the optimiser may remove allocations, so count what the optimised build does.
recipes.gotchas: Vec promises no growth strategy, so never predict capacities. Whether a grown block moves is the allocator's choice: GlobalAlloc's provided realloc allocates a new block, copies and frees the old one, so under such an allocator growth always moves (the check). Code that works because an allocator happened to grow in place is still UB. Emptying a Vec and refilling it to the same length incurs no allocator calls. The wasm allocator and memory.grow belong to wave 3.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs keeps the snapshot in `static mut SOLVER`'s `snapshot: Vec<u8>`; rebuild_snapshot() clears and refills it every quantum, so capacity persists and the buffer moves only when a quantum's snapshot is longer than every earlier one (more contact pairs or points). snapshot_ptr() and snapshot_len() are valid only until the next solver_* call; build.mjs's snapshotBytes() reads both after the call and copies with .slice(), which is right. The same rule binds T2's restore_ptr(): if the input buffer is a Vec sized to len, JS must take the pointer after the sizing call, never before.
recipes.verify_note: Vec/GlobalAlloc/realloc/global.rs confirmed verbatim; snapshot_ptr/len read-after-call matches build.mjs exactly. Check#3's 'compiles silently' claim lacks no_warnings:true; verified myself (stderr empty) -- same gap as the unsafecell lane.

corrections.claim: Check#3 ('...compiles silently: the raw pointer is on you') has no `no_warnings:true`, so the gate only checks returncode 0. I ran it via compile_oracle myself: stderr_head is empty, so true today but not structurally enforced.

lanes.title: Performance & profiling
lanes.verifier_note: Checked all 10 recipes' 57 source-warrant occurrences (~50 unique URLs) by retrieval against doc.rust-lang.org, docs.rs, github.com, v8.dev, nodejs.org, webassembly.github.io, blog.rust-lang.org and nnethercote's perf-book; checked all six engine_note claims against the live si-rpg-engine repo via gh api (solver/Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, src/rapier_law.rs, build.mjs, FLAGS.md, Cargo.lock); and ran the lane's full compile_oracle.py suite plus 20+ of my own counter-examples directly against rustc 1.98.1, including the obscure ones (E0518's retirement text, E0463 on wasm32 -Cprofile-generate, E0587/E0589, the IEEE kernel's exact hex bits reproduced on host and wasm32, and this host's own 'arrowlake-s' target-cpu=native feature counts, which matched the recipe's claimed 38-vs-5 numbers exactly). Mid-task, a relayed message claimed the input had been regenerated with additional no_warnings/wasm_no_imports check fields; I independently diffed the live file rather than trust the claim, and found only three added no_warnings:true fields (recipe 1 check 2, recipe 4 check 3, recipe 9 check 5) with no wasm_no_imports anywhere in this lane — my full-lane oracle run had already been executed against that current file and passed all three cleanly. Every source resolved and supported its claim; every engine fact matched the live repository verbatim; all 41 oracle checks passed; nothing was found stale, mismatched, fabricated or unfindable. The systemic weakness is structural, not factual: as a performance lane, its central practical numbers (V8 timings, byte-size deltas, wasm sample-percentage splits) are single-machine, single-scene, unreproducible-by-a-verifier measurements -- properly scoped throughout (rep counts, sampling intervals, and noise bounds are stated) but resting on trust in the research agent's own measurement process, since no citation or compiler check can confirm a wall-clock number. Recipe 8 (profile-the-law-natively) is the sharpest instance: it carries zero compiler checks, so every one of its claims is anchored by documentation and engine facts alone, never by executable proof.

recipes.name: Benchmark before tuning: criterion or divan with harness = false, black_box on every input and output
recipes.what: Stable Rust has no built-in bench harness (#[bench] is nightly-only), so time work with criterion 0.8 or divan 0.1 under [[bench]] harness = false and route inputs and results through std::hint::black_box so the optimizer cannot fold the measured work away.
recipes.how: Cargo.toml: `[[bench]] name = "quantum"` + `harness = false`, dev-dependency `criterion = "0.8"` (`criterion_group!` / `criterion_main!`, `c.bench_function("solver_step", |b| b.iter(|| step(black_box(&scene))))`) or `divan = "0.1"` (`#[divan::bench]` + `divan::main()`; divan 0.1.21 needs Rust 1.80+, and its `AllocProfiler` measures GlobalAlloc usage). Import `std::hint::black_box` (stable 1.66, const since 1.86): criterion 0.8.2 deprecates `criterion::black_box` with 'use `std::hint::black_box()` instead'. Wrap inputs so they are not treated as known constants and wrap outputs so a pure call is not deleted, as the two examples in the std docs do. `cargo bench` uses the `bench` profile, which inherits `release`. Time a whole unit (load a fixed scene, then N quanta inside the timed region), warm up first, and compare medians of interleaved runs. Checks can prove behaviour, never a speedup.
recipes.gotchas: black_box is best-effort: the std docs say programs cannot rely on it for correctness beyond behaving as the identity function and it gives no constant-time guarantee, so never use it to enforce behaviour. `#![feature(test)]` + `#[bench]` is rejected on stable with E0554. The bench profile follows [profile.release], so a size-tuned release profile slows benches too. Desktop timing is noisy: in the V8 runs below, three 25-rep medians of one unchanged artifact were 17.10, 17.75 and 24.82 ms, so one run proves nothing; interleave variants and repeat. A debug build is meaningless for tuning (opt-level 0 made the product scene 30x slower in V8).
recipes.engine_note: The solver has no bench today and its crate-type is cdylib only. In a scratch copy with crate-type ["cdylib", "rlib"], an example linked the law, called `step` and `bodies_ptr` directly, and reached the rapier_law exports through an `extern "C"` block because `mod rapier_law` is private. Baseline on this rig (pinned profile, V8 in node 22.22.3): 17.6 ms per 400 quanta of `solver_step` for a 13-body scene, 203 us per 400 quanta of the box law `step`.
recipes.verify_note: std docs verbatim: identity fn, best-effort, stable 1.66.0/const 1.86.0. Oracle (rustc 1.98.1): const-item black_box compiles warning-free (no_warnings gate); #![feature(test)]+#[bench] fails E0554; input/output loop runs, prints 2.

recipes.name: Choose release-profile knobs by measurement: opt-level sets speed; lto, codegen-units, strip, debug move bytes
recipes.what: Measured on a scratch copy of the solver (wasm32, V8): only opt-level changed speed materially (s 1.69x, z 2.73x, 0 30x slower); lto, codegen-units, debug, strip and panic moved size between -12% and +634% within run-to-run noise on speed. Cargo's lto = false is thin-local LTO, a no-op at codegen-units = 1, and release strips debuginfo by default.
recipes.how: Method: `cargo +1.98.1 build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --offline --locked --config 'profile.release.<knob>=<value>'` with build.mjs's RUSTFLAGS, then size and V8 time (median of 3 interleaved rounds of 25-rep medians after 5 warm-up reps). Pinned profile: 1,524,412 bytes (code section 1,285,550; name section 182,205), 17.6 ms per 400 product quanta. opt-level 2: -2.2%, 1.02x. "s": -0.8% file, -13.2% code, 1.69x slower. "z": -4.8% file, -34.9% code, 2.73x slower. 0: +228%, 30x slower. lto "thin": +4.6%; "fat": -6.4%; "off": +17 bytes; codegen-units 16: +13.3%; all within noise on time. debug = "line-tables-only": 11,192,335 bytes (DWARF), same speed. strip = "symbols": -12.0% (name section gone); strip = "none": 3,245,410 bytes (std's DWARF). Put profiling settings in a custom profile (`[profile.profiling] inherits = "release"`, `debug = "line-tables-only"`) so the pinned one never changes. Measure the build itself: `cargo build --timings` writes target/cargo-timings/cargo-timing.html (per-unit time, codegen time, concurrency); `cargo llvm-lines` counts LLVM IR lines and copies per generic function (the monomorphization cost that codegen-units and LTO trade against); `cargo bloat --release --crates` sizes native binaries only (its README: 'WASM is not supported. Use twiggy instead.'); twiggy's repository is archived (read-only), so for wasm also read section sizes directly.
recipes.gotchas: `lto = false` is not `lto = "off"`: the Cargo Book defines false as thin local LTO across the crate's codegen units and says no LTO is performed at codegen-units 1 or opt-level 0, yet switching to "off" still produced a different artifact (see the digest recipe). s/z are 'not necessarily smaller' (Cargo Book): s cut the code section 13% but the file only 0.8% because less inlining left more functions to name (name section 182,205 -> 338,450 bytes; z: 550,418), so count the whole file. The rustc Book says z often gives larger binaries than s; here z was smaller, so measure. The Cargo Book's profile table lists strip = "none" for release, but since 1.77 profiles without debuginfo get strip = "debuginfo", and `cargo build -v` on 1.98.1 shows `-C strip=debuginfo` on the solver; writing strip = "none" pulls std's DWARF back in. Tests, benchmarks, build scripts and proc macros ignore `panic`. rustc run by hand defaults to opt-level 0, which also turns on cfg(debug_assertions).
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml's profile (opt-level 3, lto = false, codegen-units 1, panic = "abort", overflow-checks = false) is at the fast end of every variant measured. Its lto = false means no LTO at all at codegen-units 1, and panic = "abort" restates the target default (`rustc --print cfg --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` prints panic="abort"), so that line only matters for a native host build of the law. The 182,205-byte name section is 12% of the artifact and is what gives V8 profiles readable frames (profiling recipe).
recipes.verify_note: 9/9 sources verbatim-matched incl. rustc Book's 'z often larger than s'. gh api confirms solver/Cargo.toml [profile.release] = opt-level 3/lto false/cgu 1/panic abort/overflow-checks false, byte for byte. Oracle: all 5 checks pass.

recipes.name: Split profile knobs into digest-only and result-changing before editing the solver's pinned release profile
recipes.what: On a scratch copy of solver/, 15 profile variants all changed the wasm digest and even the code section, yet all gave byte-identical results over 400 quanta of both laws; knobs change results only through semantics: overflow-checks, debug-assertions, cfg(target_feature) paths, NaN bit patterns and std transcendentals.
recipes.how: Copy solver/{Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, rust-toolchain.toml, .cargo/config.toml, src/} to scratch and build with build.mjs's RUSTFLAGS (-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd plus the three --remap-path-prefix) and `--config 'profile.release.<knob>=<value>'`. Drive each artifact through one scene from JS: product law (floor + rotated ramp, 12 dynamic boxes, 1 driven character; solver_load, then 400 solver_step with SHA-256 over every snapshot and the final bodies) and box law (16 bodies, 4 colliders, 400 step). Variants: opt-level 0/2/s/z, lto off/thin/fat, codegen-units 16, debug line-tables-only, strip symbols/none, panic unwind, overflow-checks true, debug-assertions true, +simd128. Result hashes 10041692ff2e6d8b / a2a26a5471e435ba for all 16 artifacts, 400/400 steps accepted, no trap. Rebuilding the pinned profile last reproduced the first digest byte for byte (b21c7f15..., Windows bytes). Why even inert knobs move bytes: Cargo passes a different -C metadata per profile (lto = false: si_solver 648e556cfabde42d, rapier rlib 5f1f6bff601edb82; lto = "off": 5d66e6efdb52edec, d945852ad0d5ae49), and the name, code and data sections all changed, consistent with the metadata feeding symbol and type hashes (mechanism inferred, not traced). Classify: digest-only (measured): opt-level, lto, codegen-units, debug, strip, panic (the target forces abort), +simd128. Result-changing by construction: overflow-checks (an overflow becomes a panic, a trap under abort, instead of a wrapped value), debug-assertions (compiles every crate's debug_assert! in: code +12.4%), target features (cfg-gated paths), and anything that changes how a transcendental is evaluated. The checks show each mechanism on std code; the IEEE kernel gives identical bits at opt-level 0, 3, z + fat LTO and s + 16 units, on the host and in wasm.
recipes.gotchas: RFC 3514 keeps one latitude in IEEE operations: NaN bit patterns are non-deterministic and may differ between compile-time and run-time evaluation, so an optimization change can move a NaN's bits; refuse or canonicalise NaN before anything is hashed. std documents sin, cos, exp, powf and friends as having unspecified precision that can differ even between invocations in one execution, so inlining or folding them differently is allowed to change results. overflow-checks = false is already the release default; wrapping_* methods ignore the knob, plain `+` does not. One scene is evidence, not proof: overflow-checks and debug-assertions did not trap here, which says nothing about other scenes. Any edit to the profile, including one that changes no codegen, is a new artifact that needs a new pin.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml [profile.release] and fixtures/solver.sha256: any profile edit, even lto = false -> "off" (no more LTO than today), moves every crate's -C metadata and therefore the digest; the golden hash is the invariant that must not move, so rerun the golden suite and re-pin the Linux digest together. Keep overflow-checks and debug-assertions off in the artifact (turning them on changes the law's failure mode, not only its bytes), and keep the target-feature set pinned (-relaxed-simd; +simd128 kept this scene's results but is another artifact). rapier_law.rs refuses NaN in poses and velocities (write_body, bad) and mix_u64 uses wrapping_mul/wrapping_add, so neither NaN payloads nor the overflow-checks knob reaches those paths.
recipes.verify_note: Self-ran the IEEE kernel (rustc 1.98.1): identical hex bits at opt-level 0, opt-level 3+cgu1, and on wasm32 -- 20.873008230947335 every time. gh api: engine's real mix_u64/write_body match the wrapping/NaN-refusal claims verbatim.

recipes.name: Leave inlining to rustc: #[inline] for cross-crate calls, #[cold] on refusal paths, static dispatch when hot
recipes.what: Every #[inline] form is a hint the compiler may ignore; since 1.75 rustc makes small leaf functions cross-crate-inlinable by itself; #[cold] marks unlikely paths; generics are monomorphized into static calls while dyn Trait calls go through a vtable that blocks inlining.
recipes.how: Within one crate at opt-level 3, private helpers inline without attributes. Across crates without LTO a non-generic function inlines only if it is marked #[inline] or, since 1.75 (rust-lang/rust#116505), if it is a small leaf whose optimized MIR contains no calls or asserts. Use #[inline] on small non-leaf functions of a library that other crates call in hot loops. Split an entry point into a small hot path and a `#[cold] #[inline(never)]` refusal path so the hot path stays small (perf book). Dispatch: a generic `fn f<S: Shape>(xs: &[S])` is monomorphized, so there is no runtime cost and calls can inline; `&[Box<dyn Shape>]` looks up each call in the vtable carried in a two-word fat pointer, and the Book says dynamic dispatch 'prevents the compiler from choosing to inline a method's code'. For a closed set of kinds, an enum + match is static dispatch without one copy per type. Measure with cargo-llvm-lines if monomorphization inflates compile time.
recipes.rust_version: any; automatic cross-crate inlining of small leaf functions 1.75+
recipes.gotchas: #[inline(always)] is still only a suggestion in the Reference, and the Reference warns that poor inlining decisions slow programs down. On 1.98.1, #[inline] on a struct is rejected with 'attribute cannot be used on structs' and no error code (`rustc +1.98.1 --explain E0518` says that code is no longer emitted: match the message, not a code). Tiny leaf functions no longer need #[inline] for cross-crate inlining; small functions that call something still do in non-LTO builds. Inlining changes bytes and speed, not IEEE results (digest recipe).
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs's helpers (field, body_at, js_min, js_max, rank, resolve_pair) are private and share one crate at codegen-units 1. Measured: the optimized box-law module defines only bodies_ptr, colliders_ptr and step, and step's remaining calls are LLVM intrinsics (llvm.is.fpclass, llvm.sqrt, lifetime markers). No attribute is needed. The law has no dyn of its own; parry3d-f64 0.30.2's SharedShape is `pub struct SharedShape(pub Arc<dyn Shape>)`, so narrow-phase shape dispatch is dynamic inside the dependency (DefaultQueryDispatcher was a top V8 frame), outside the engine's control.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle: #[inline] on a struct fails w/ rustc's exact wording, NO error code -- confirms E0518 'no longer emitted'. Dispatch-size check ran exact '3 3 3 16 8'. Hot/cold #[cold] pattern compiles warning-free (no_warnings gate).

recipes.name: Prove indices once: an entry guard, chunks_exact_mut or as_chunks_mut removes per-iteration bounds checks
recipes.what: Measured in LLVM IR at opt-level 3: LLVM already hoists the check out of a loop without stores, but a read-modify-write loop keeps one check per iteration; chunks_exact_mut and as_chunks_mut (1.88) leave none, and in the solver the early `n_bodies > MAX_BODIES` return is what removes all 30 checks from the box law's step.
recipes.how: Measure: `rustc +1.98.1 --crate-type lib -C opt-level=3 -C codegen-units=1 -C panic=abort --emit=llvm-ir x.rs` (host and --target wasm32-unknown-unknown gave the same counts) and count `panic_bounds_check` calls per function and whether they sit inside the loop. `for i in 0..n { s += v[i] }`: one check hoisted before the loop (loop unrolled 8x). `let v = &v[..n];` or `assert!(n <= v.len());` first: one check before the loop, none in it. `v.iter().take(n)`: none. Stride-17 read-modify-write `b[i * 17 + 4] = ...`: one check per iteration inside the loop, not unrolled. The same loop over `b.chunks_exact_mut(17)` or `b.as_chunks_mut::<17>().0`: none. The engine's own `step` (lib.rs minus `mod rapier_law;`): 0 checks as written; with the up-front guard deleted, 30 `panic_bounds_check` call sites and 1,055 IR lines instead of 759. Idioms: guard or slice once at entry (`let rows = &mut buf[..n * STRIDE];`), then iterate rows with chunks_exact_mut(STRIDE) or as_chunks_mut::<STRIDE>(), whose `&mut [f64; STRIDE]` rows make constant indices check-free. `get_unchecked` is the perf book's 'last resort' and needs a SAFETY argument.
recipes.gotchas: A check inside a storing loop also blocks unrolling and vectorization (the stride loop stayed one element per iteration), so it costs more than the compare. chunks_exact skips the tail silently: the last up to chunk_size-1 elements are only in `.remainder()`, so assert it is empty when the layout must be exact. Checks come back when the guard moves after the loop or when the bound comes from a value the optimizer cannot relate to the slice (measured: 30). In these measurements LLVM hoisted the check only out of the loop without stores; the storing loop kept it at every iteration. Indexing a value the compiler cannot prove in range still panics at run time (exit 101 below).
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs `step` checks `n_bodies > MAX_BODIES || n_colliders > MAX_COLLIDERS` before touching the fixed-length statics, and that single guard lets LLVM prove every `field(bodies, i, slot)` and `colliders[j * COLLIDER_STRIDE + k]` index. Keep a guard like it first in every new export (T2's solver_restore included). rapier_law.rs `body_at` / `collider_at` copy rows with an index loop; `as_chunks::<BODY_STRIDE>()` would express a row directly, but that is a code change the golden hash must confirm, not a measured win.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle ran all 3 checks on rustc 1.98.1: as_chunks/get() output, guard+as_chunks_mut(65-refused), and OOB-index panic(101) all matched exactly. gh api: engine's real step() guard is verbatim 'n_bodies as usize > MAX_BODIES'.

recipes.name: Reuse per-quantum buffers: clear() keeps capacity, with_capacity sizes once, SmallVec/ArrayVec for small lists
recipes.what: Vec never shrinks on its own, and refilling a cleared Vec to the same length 'should incur no calls to the allocator', so a buffer cleared each quantum stops allocating once it reaches its peak; SmallVec keeps up to N items inline and spills to the heap; ArrayVec has a hard capacity and never allocates.
recipes.how: Size once: `Vec::with_capacity(n)` holds at least n elements without reallocating, and vec![x; n] / with_capacity(n) request exactly n elements from the allocator. Reuse: keep the Vec in long-lived state and `clear()` it at the start of each quantum (perf book: clear empties the Vec 'without affecting its capacity'); truncate also keeps capacity; shrink_to_fit gives memory back. Small bounded lists: `SmallVec<[T; N]>` (smallvec 1.16.2) stores N inline and reports `spilled()`; `ArrayVec<T, CAP>` (arrayvec 0.7.8) is backed by a fixed array, push panics when full, try_push returns an error. Measured below: a spilled SmallVec keeps its heap buffer across clear(), and ArrayVec<u32, 4> is 20 bytes. Count allocations before and after a change (divan's AllocProfiler; DHAT on Linux) and profile first: allocation is often not the cost.
recipes.gotchas: A reused buffer's pointer is stable only while it does not grow; growth reallocates and Vec promises no particular growth strategy, so any raw pointer handed out must be re-read after each call (memory-layout lane). clear() on a spilled SmallVec keeps the heap allocation; it does not return to inline storage. SmallVec is slightly slower than Vec per operation because it checks where its data lives (perf book), so use it only where it removes allocations. ArrayVec::push panics on overflow, which is a trap in a panic = abort wasm module; use try_push and return a status. with_capacity counts elements, not bytes.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `rebuild_snapshot` already reuses `SOLVER.snapshot` with `out.clear()`, so the snapshot stops allocating after its largest contact set. Allocations left per quantum: `integrate` builds `plans` and a `collisions` Vec per driven body, `rebuild_snapshot` collects `pairs`, and `solver_clear_warmstart` builds `ptrs`. Measured: in a V8 profile of the scene (100 us sampling, 1,192 wasm samples) the allocator (dlmalloc) took 0.7% and the law's own code 4.0%, so reusing these buffers would be tidiness, not a speed lever, and would still move the digest.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle ran all 3 checks (real smallvec/arrayvec crates, rustc 1.98.1): clear()-keeps-capacity, SmallVec-spill+ArrayVec-refuse, with_capacity-exact all matched. gh api confirms the named allocation sites verbatim.

recipes.name: Lay out hot data by access: struct-of-arrays when loops read few fields, rows sized against cache lines
recipes.what: Struct-of-arrays lets a loop load only the fields it reads; array-of-structs keeps one element's fields together; either way the sizes come from size_of / align_of and #[repr(align(N))], and cache-line sizes are per-architecture guesses (crossbeam assumes 128 bytes on x86_64 and aarch64, 64 on most others).
recipes.how: Know the numbers before choosing: `[T; N]` has size `size_of::<T>() * N` and T's alignment, and a size is always a multiple of its alignment; repr(Rust) guarantees only that fields are aligned, so use repr(C) when a layout is an ABI. Raise alignment with `#[repr(align(64))]` (a power of two up to 2^29; not combinable with packed). SoA in Rust is one Vec per field (or a derive such as soa_derive 0.14.0, which generates a Vec per field) and loops that zip the fields they need; soa_derive states the main advantage is loading only some fields when iterating. Keep hot types small: the perf book notes types larger than 128 bytes are copied with memcpy rather than inline code, and smaller types reduce memory traffic and cache pressure. Cache-line padding (crossbeam-utils CachePadded) exists to stop false sharing between threads.
recipes.gotchas: SoA gives up indexing into one element as a struct (soa_derive's generated vector cannot be indexed into a reference) and turns a one-element copy into scattered loads. repr(Rust) may reorder fields, so never compute offsets by hand without repr(C). There is no std constant for the cache-line size; crossbeam calls its per-architecture values reasonable guesses. On 1.98.1 a non-power-of-two alignment is E0589 and packed + align is E0587. Changing a layout that crosses an ABI is an interface change, not an optimization.
recipes.engine_note: The solver ABI is array-of-structs: BODIES is [f64; 64 x 17] = 8,704 bytes, 136 bytes per body (2.125 64-byte lines, so rows straddle lines), and build.mjs hard-codes the stride 17 and every offset. rapier_law.rs `body_at` returns [f64; 17] = 136 bytes by value, just over the perf book's 128-byte memcpy size. The V8 profile of the scene put 65% of wasm samples in parry and Rapier and 4.0% in the law's own code, so there is no measured case for changing the ABI layout.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle ran the size/align check (136/8/8704/64/64) exact match, plus E0589 (non-pow2 align) and E0587 (packed+align) exact on rustc 1.98.1. gh api: engine's real BODIES=[f64;64*17]=8704 bytes matches verbatim.

recipes.name: Profile the law natively (samply, perf, VTune, Superluminal), then confirm hot spots with node --cpu-prof
recipes.what: A native build of the same crate replayed the scene with byte-identical results and ran 1.9x faster than the wasm in V8, but it takes a different square-root path, so rank Rust hot spots natively and confirm them with V8's profile of the shipped artifact, which names wasm frames only when the name section is kept.
recipes.how: Profiling build: `[profile.profiling] inherits = "release"` + `debug = "line-tables-only"` (line tables only: file and line info for backtraces), plus `-C force-frame-pointers=yes` for frame-pointer unwinding (perf book). Tools: samply (`cargo install --locked samply`; `samply record ./target/profiling/<bin>`; macOS, Linux, Windows; Firefox Profiler UI); cargo-flamegraph (`cargo flamegraph`; perf on Linux, xctrace on macOS, blondie or dtrace on Windows); perf (Linux, hardware counters; view in Hotspot or Firefox Profiler); Intel VTune (Windows, Linux, macOS); Superluminal (Windows, Xbox, PlayStation and Linux per its page; recommends release `debug = true`; the superluminal-perf 0.4.0 events compile out on non-Windows); Tracy through tracy-client 0.19.0 (`span!` zones, `frame_mark()`, feature `enable` = TRACY_ENABLE). Native vs V8, measured on this rig with the pinned profile: native x86_64-pc-windows-msvc 9.3 ms per 400 product quanta and 150 us per 400 box steps vs V8 17.6 ms and 203 us; result streams (2,045,632 + 870,400 bytes) identical. In V8: `node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-interval 100 app.mjs` writes a .cpuprofile (default interval 1000 us); V8 runs wasm in Liftoff first and recompiles hot functions with TurboFan in the background, so warm up before measuring. With the 182,205-byte name section, frames read like `_RNv...si_solver10rapier_law6ensure` (v0-mangled; rustfilt demangles); the strip = "symbols" build showed only `wasm-function[N]`. On Linux, V8's `--perf-prof` flag (with `--interpreted-frames-native-stack`) lets perf attribute samples to JIT-compiled frames.
recipes.gotchas: The native build is a proxy with a different mix: libm 0.2.16 takes the hardware sqrtsd path wherever sse2 is enabled but its software path on wasm32 unless the unstable-intrinsics feature is on (the solver resolves libm with only default + arch: `cargo tree -e features -i libm`), and in V8 that software sqrt plus the 128-bit multiply it calls (__multi3) took 22% of wasm samples, cost a native profile cannot show. Speed ratios differ by law (1.9x product, 1.35x box). strip = "symbols" saves 12% of the artifact but blinds V8 profiles. Keep profiler crates and their `enable` features out of the pinned build (a feature changes the artifact), and note Tracy may broadcast discovery packets on the local network. At the default 1 ms interval a 400-quantum scene yields only about 80 samples; run longer or sample faster.
recipes.engine_note: Profile natively from a scratch or bench build of solver/ with crate-type ["cdylib", "rlib"], never from the pinned profile, replaying input bits dumped from the JS run so the native run computes the same record (identical here). Then confirm with node --cpu-prof on build.mjs's artifact. Measured V8 split (100 us sampling, 1,192 wasm samples): parry3d_f64 34.9%, rapier3d_f64 30.3%, libm 13.9% (sqrt), __multi3 8.4% (called only from libm's sqrt), nalgebra 4.6%, the law's own code 4.0%, dlmalloc 0.7%. The software sqrt comes from `enhanced-determinism` (rapier: simba/libm_force; parry: simba/libm_force, glamx/libm, glamx/scalar-math); whether the wasm f64.sqrt instruction could replace it without moving results is for the float-determinism lane, not a flag to flip here.

recipes.name: Get SIMD on stable from auto-vectorization, std::arch and #[target_feature]; std::simd is still nightly-only
recipes.what: Once a SIMD feature is enabled, LLVM vectorizes elementwise loops and integer reductions but keeps float reductions in order; std::arch intrinsics are safe #[target_feature] functions that need `unsafe` unless the caller itself enables the feature (on wasm they are always safe to call); std::simd (portable_simd) needs nightly.
recipes.how: Measured on wasm32 (`--emit=asm`, opt-level 3): without a flag all three loops are scalar; with `-C target-feature=+simd128`, `y[i] = y[i] + a * x[i]` becomes f64x2.mul / f64x2.add, a wrapping i64 sum becomes i64x2.add, and an f64 sum stays nine sequential f64.add (unrolled, never reassociated). Enable per function with `#[target_feature(enable = "simd128")]` or per crate with `-C target-feature=+simd128`; the flag does not rebuild the precompiled std, and wasm has no runtime detection, so a module either has SIMD and needs an engine with SIMD or has none. x86 native: runtime dispatch with `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")` and a `#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")]` fn called in `unsafe` (safe functions may carry the attribute since 1.86). Measured on 1.98.1: `_mm_add_pd` (SSE2, in the host's default features) from a plain fn is E0133; from a `#[target_feature(enable = "sse2")]` fn it compiles without unsafe. `#![feature(portable_simd)]` is E0554 on stable (tracking issue rust-lang/rust#86656).
recipes.rust_version: safe #[target_feature] fns 1.86+; wasm32 simd128 intrinsics stable; std::simd nightly-only
recipes.gotchas: Relaxed-SIMD intrinsics such as f64x2_relaxed_madd have implementation-specific results (core::arch::wasm32 docs); the pinned build disables relaxed-simd and another lane owns the opcode lint. Rewriting a float reduction into lanes changes its result; LLVM will not do it for you, so a law must not do it silently. rustc calls -C target-feature unsafe (undefined behaviour on a CPU without the feature). A target feature enabled only by the global target default did not count as 'the caller enables' on 1.98.1 (E0133 for SSE2): annotate the caller.
recipes.engine_note: The solver builds with no SIMD feature and -relaxed-simd (FLAGS.md). A +simd128 build of the scratch copy gave identical results on the scene, 1,478,802 bytes (-3.0%), a target_features section of 157 instead of 148 bytes, and 0.95x V8 time (inside the +-10% noise). The small change is consistent with glam 0.33.10 (the version glamx 0.3.1 uses) keeping its simd128 paths in f32 and bool types (0 target_feature cfgs under src/f64). SIMD is not worth a new digest today.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle ran all 8 checks on rustc 1.98.1: portable_simd->E0554, target_feature-caller->E0133, SSE2 outside/inside target_feature->E0133/compiles-warning-free (no_warnings gate), plus 3 wasm simd128 checks -- all matched exactly.

recipes.name: Keep target-cpu=native, PGO and BOLT out of the pinned artifact: they tie codegen to a machine or a profile
recipes.what: target-cpu=native targets 'the processor of the host machine' and turns on its features (38 instead of 5 on this rig), which flips any cfg(target_feature) path such as wide 1.7.1's fused mul_add; for wasm32, rustc 1.98.1 ignores it with warnings. PGO bytes depend on a training run and cannot even be instrumented for wasm32-unknown-unknown (E0463 profiler_builtins); BOLT rewrites only x86-64 and AArch64 ELF.
recipes.how: Measured: `rustc +1.98.1 --print cfg -C target-cpu=native` on this host (rustc names it arrowlake-s) lists 38 target_feature entries against 5 by default (cmpxchg16b, fxsr, sse, sse2, sse3), adding avx, avx2, fma, bmi1/2 and more. For wasm32, `-C target-cpu=native` printed "'arrowlake-s' is not a recognized processor for this target (ignoring processor)" plus one ignored-feature warning per x86 feature, and the code section was byte-identical to the default build (the file differed only in the module name, which follows the output filename); `--print target-cpus --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` lists bleeding-edge, generic (default), lime1 and mvp. The checks show the mechanism: a cfg(target_feature = "fma") branch prints the fused 2^-54 with +fma and 0 without, while plain a * b + c prints 0 both ways (no contraction). wide 1.7.1's f64x2::mul_add documents the same split (vfmadd single rounding with FMA, vfmaq_f64 on ARM64 NEON, (self * m) + a two roundings otherwise). PGO: rustc's four steps are -Cprofile-generate, run, llvm-profdata merge, -Cprofile-use (cargo-pgo wraps them and BOLT); `-Cprofile-generate` with --target wasm32-unknown-unknown fails with error[E0463]: can't find crate for `profiler_builtins`. BOLT 'operates on X86-64 and AArch64 ELF binaries'. For any native build of the law, pin the target CPU explicitly (never native) and record it next to the digest.
recipes.gotchas: A native binary may use instructions other CPUs lack: std::arch says to run a feature-enabled binary only on systems with the feature, and rustc calls -C target-feature unsafe. PGO output is 'optimized with respect to the profiled workloads' (cargo-pgo), so a different training run gives different bytes and a different workload can even run slower; profiles go stale as code changes. That PGO or BOLT cannot change IEEE results is an inference from the float semantics, not measured here, because wasm could not be instrumented. Do not count on wasm32 ignoring native forever: it is a warning today, and an unpinned flag in RUSTFLAGS is still an unpinned input.
recipes.engine_note: The wasm artifact is untouched by the builder's CPU today (native is ignored for wasm32 on 1.98.1) and cannot be PGO-instrumented. The real exposure is the planned native host bindings (Godot, then Unreal), where native or +fma flips cfg(target_feature) paths. In the pinned graph those sit in wide (reached through simba 0.10.2) and in glam's f32 types; rapier3d-f64 0.35.3, parry3d-f64 0.30.2, glamx 0.3.1, nalgebra 0.35.0 and simba 0.10.2 have 0 such cfg lines. aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu enables neon by default, so an ARM64 native build selects wide's fused path wherever it is reached. A native law must pin its CPU baseline and match the wasm golden.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced on this rig: target-cpu=native gives 'arrowlake-s not recognized...ignoring' + 38 ignored features vs 5 default (exact counts). -Cprofile-generate on wasm32 fails E0463 'profiler_builtins' exactly as claimed.

lanes.title: What changed in Rust 1.80 → 1.98 and edition 2024
lanes.verifier_note: Checked all 53 warrant sources by direct retrieval (17 dated 'Announcing Rust 1.NN.0' posts 1.80-1.98, 3 topic blog posts, the current edition guide's 2024 chapter across 12 pages, the current rustc book and Cargo book, current std/core docs, and two RELEASES.md snapshots) plus roughly 20 uncited 'stabilized in 1.NN' claims scattered through gotchas (LazyCell 1.80, Vec::extract_if 1.87, array_windows 1.94, Box::new_zeroed 1.92, assert_matches! 1.96, cargo info 1.82, publish --workspace 1.90, build.build-dir/--target host-tuple 1.91, resolver.lockfile-path 1.97, cargo fix target-selection 1.89, dangerous_implicit_autorefs added-1.88/deny-1.89, etc.) via independent search. Also ran every check in checks[] myself through scripts/compile_oracle.py against the real pinned rustc 1.98.1 (host, wasm32-unknown-unknown and wasm32v1-none): 58/58 passed. Also checked every engine_note claim against si-rpg-engine@main via gh api (lib.rs, rapier_law.rs, Cargo.toml, .cargo/config.toml, rust-toolchain.toml, build.mjs) byte-for-byte, including all 7 static_mut_refs line numbers and all 10 #[no_mangle] export names. Result: zero source misattributions, zero stale APIs, zero check/prose mismatches, zero wrong engine facts across all 10 recipes. Systemic weakness: this lane's two verification paths (citation retrieval and the compile oracle) both have a blind spot the recipes exploit unintentionally — precise-looking measured numbers in gotchas that are neither cited nor exercised by any checks[] entry. Recipe 4's gotcha claims the relaxed-simd fused-multiply-add 'returned the fused result... (-8.67e-19 where a separate multiply and add give 0)', but check #6 in that same recipe only asserts the function compiles and exports 'fused' — it never asserts that stdout value, so the specific number is untested by the very check sitting next to it. Recipe 1's gotchas cite exact digest prefixes and a '22 bytes' delta from a blank-line probe with no matching check and no source at all. These are plausible (spec text for algebraic_*/relaxed-simd explicitly allows codegen-dependent results, so the shape of the claim is right) but unfalsifiable by anyone reading only this lane's artifacts; they rest entirely on an unlogged local run.

recipes.name: Move si-solver to edition 2024: cargo fix rewrites 10 #[no_mangle], hand-fix 7 static_mut_refs
recipes.what: On 1.98.1, `cargo fix --edition` on a copy of solver/ changed only the 10 `#[no_mangle]` exports to `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`, left `edition = "2021"` in Cargo.toml, and left 7 `static_mut_refs` sites that fail the build once the edition is 2024; neither rewrite changed a byte of the wasm (measured).
recipes.how: 1) `cargo +1.98.1 fix --edition --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (needs a clean git tree or --allow-dirty): it rewrites 3 attributes in lib.rs and 7 in rapier_law.rs and prints the 7 static_mut_refs warnings it cannot fix. `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` compiles warning-free on edition 2021 since 1.82, so this step can land on its own. 2) Set `edition = "2024"` by hand. 3) Rewrite the 7 sites without moving any line: lib.rs:28/33 and rapier_law.rs:78 `unsafe { X.as_mut_ptr() }` -> `(&raw mut X).cast::<f64>()` (taking `&raw` of a static mut is safe since 1.82, no unsafe block); lib.rs:183/184 `&mut BODIES` / `&COLLIDERS` -> `&mut *(&raw mut BODIES)` / `&*(&raw const COLLIDERS)`; rapier_law.rs:738/743 `SOLVER.snapshot.as_ptr()` / `.len()` -> `(*(&raw const SOLVER)).snapshot.as_ptr()` / `.len()`. Whether those references are sound is the unsafe-ffi lane's question; this recipe states what the compiler now demands (checked: a solver-shaped module written this way builds warning-free under 2024, imports nothing, and its step and snapshot exports work). 4) Rebuild through build.mjs and compare the digest.
recipes.gotchas: Under 2024 static_mut_refs is a deny-by-default lint, not a hard error: the compiler reports `#[deny(static_mut_refs)]` (part of rust_2024_compatibility) and `#![allow(static_mut_refs)]` makes the crate build (checked), so an allow is a wrong fix that still compiles. There is no automatic migration for it. Explicit `&X` / `&mut X`, `ref` bindings and autoref method calls such as `.as_mut_ptr()`, `.as_ptr()` and `.len()` are flagged; by-value indexing such as `BODIES[base + k]` and `HEIGHTS[i]` is not (checked). Byte identity holds only while panicking code keeps its line: the module embeds panic locations, and a blank line inserted at the top of rapier_law.rs changed 22 bytes (digest b03c2b70...) while the same shift in lib.rs changed none (measured), so a reflow by `cargo fmt` under style_edition 2024 can move the digest without changing behaviour. Identity was measured on the Windows host (sha256 b21c7f15... for 2021, for 2024 with the lint allowed, and for 2024 with the &raw rewrite), not against the Linux pin.
recipes.engine_note: The 10 attribute sites are the exports in solver/src/lib.rs (bodies_ptr, colliders_ptr, step) and solver/src/rapier_law.rs (heights_ptr, canon_zero, solver_load, solver_step, snapshot_ptr, snapshot_len, solver_clear_warmstart); the 7 static_mut_refs sites are lib.rs:28, 33, 183, 184 and rapier_law.rs:78, 738, 743 in the local checkout. A line-preserving migration should leave fixtures/solver.sha256 unchanged; write T2's restore exports in the 2024 spelling from the start. The dependencies are already edition-2024 crates (rapier3d-f64 0.35.3: edition 2024, rust-version 1.86; nalgebra 0.35.0: edition 2024, rust-version 1.89.0) and editions are per crate, so the solver's own edition changes nothing inside them.
recipes.verify_note: 7/7 oracle checks pass on rustc 1.98.1. Engine: all 10 #[no_mangle] names and all 7 static_mut_refs sites (lib.rs:28,33,183,184; rapier_law.rs:78,738,743) match main byte-for-byte; Cargo.toml still edition=2021.

recipes.name: Expect edition 2024 to drop if-let scrutinee and tail-expression temporaries earlier
recipes.what: Edition 2024 drops the temporaries of an `if let` scrutinee before the `else` branch runs and drops a block's tail-expression temporaries before its local variables; both reorder `Drop` side effects (checked), and the first is why let chains (stable 1.88) are 2024-only.
recipes.how: Rules: in `if let P = e { .. } else { .. }` the temporaries of `e` now drop before `else` (2021: after the whole expression); in a tail expression they now drop before the block's locals (2021: after), so `c.borrow().len()` as the tail of the block that owns `c` compiles (E0597 in 2021). Migration: `if_let_rescope` is auto-fixed by rewriting to `match`, which keeps the 2021 order, so review each rewrite; `tail_expr_drop_order` only warns. After the switch write `if let Some(x) = a && let Ok(y) = f(x) { .. }` instead of nested if-lets. `if let` guards in match arms (`Some(s) if let Some(x) = parse(s) =>`, 1.95) are not tied to the edition: they compile in 2021 as well (checked).
recipes.rust_version: edition 2024 (1.85+); let chains 1.88 (2024 only); if-let guards 1.95 (every edition)
recipes.gotchas: The automatic `match` rewrite preserves the old, later drop, so the deadlock the edition fixes (a RwLock read guard kept alive into an `else` that takes the write lock) survives the migration unless the rewrite is undone on purpose. In 2021 a let chain is the error 'let chains are only allowed in Rust 2024 or later' (checked). Tail-expression temporaries are also sometimes no longer extended to the enclosing scope, so a borrow that compiled through extension in 2021 can fail in 2024. 1.91 applied the 2024 if-let rule to temporaries made by pin!, format_args!, write! and writeln! in 2024 scrutinees.
recipes.engine_note: cargo fix --edition on the solver copy reported no if_let_rescope or tail_expr_drop_order site (measured): `ensure()` in rapier_law.rs uses `if let Some(loaded) = solver.loaded.as_ref()` with no else, and the other matches are let-else. The rules start to matter in the planned host bindings (Godot, then Unreal), where a wrapper may hold a lock guard or RefCell borrow over the solver's static state across an if-let.
recipes.verify_note: 10/10 oracle checks pass. if-let/tail-expr drop-order pages, let-chains-2024-only wording, and the 1.91.0 pin!/format_args!/write!/writeln! restriction all matched verbatim. Engine's ensure() if-let-with-no-else confirmed on main.

recipes.name: Know which edition-2024 changes cargo fix --edition migrates and which stay manual
recipes.what: Of the Edition Guide's 2024 list, `cargo fix --edition` rewrites unsafe attributes, unsafe extern blocks, unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn, if-let (into match), RPIT over-capture (inserts `use<..>`), `expr` -> `expr_2021`, `gen` -> `r#gen`, `Box<[T]>::into_iter`, prelude collisions, reserved `#".."#` syntax, match-ergonomics patterns, `env::set_var` calls and Cargo.toml key names; it does not migrate static_mut_refs, tail-expression drop order, never-type fallback, missing macro fragment specifiers, combined doctests or the resolver change.
recipes.how: Run `cargo fix --edition` once per target and feature set that compiles distinct code (it only sees what that configuration compiles), read everything it prints, flip `edition = "2024"` by hand, then build, test and `cargo fmt`. What changes meaning: `expr` fragments now also match `const { .. }` and `_`; `-> impl Trait` captures every in-scope lifetime (narrow with `+ use<..>`, available in all editions since 1.82); `Box<[T]>::into_iter()` yields `T`, not `&T`; never-type fallback is `!`, not `()`; `extern` blocks must be `unsafe extern` with per-item `safe` / `unsafe`; unsafe operations inside an `unsafe fn` need their own `unsafe {}` (a warning); `std::env::set_var` / `remove_var` are unsafe; `gen` is reserved; `Future` / `IntoFuture` join the prelude; resolver "3" is implied; doctests are combined into one binary (opt out per test with `standalone_crate`); rustfmt's style edition follows the edition unless `style_edition` is configured separately.
recipes.gotchas: Doctests, macros and build-time generated code are not migrated. The expr_2021 rewrite exists to keep old macro matching; undoing it changes which arm matches (checked: a `const { .. }` argument picks the `$e:expr` arm in 2024 and the `const $b:block` arm in 2021). impl_trait_overcaptures cannot always fix argument-position impl Trait. Code that relied on `()` never-type fallback already fails in 2021 on 1.92+ through a deny lint and is a type error (E0277) in 2024. Doctests that assert panic Location lines or type_name output can break once doctests are combined.
recipes.engine_note: The solver has no extern blocks, unsafe fns, macros, RPIT returns, `gen` identifiers or boxed slices, so of this list only the unsafe attributes touch it (measured: cargo fix changed nothing else). The rustfmt style edition is the one item that can move the digest with no semantic change, because a reformat shifts panic-location line numbers (see the solver migration recipe).
recipes.verify_note: 11/11 oracle checks pass. All 9 sources matched verbatim; independently cross-checked uncited claims (gen->r#gen via keyword_idents_2024, Future/IntoFuture join prelude, unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn auto-fix) via search, all correct.

recipes.name: Treat wasm32-unknown-unknown's six default features as byte changes, and -relaxed-simd as no ban
recipes.what: On 1.98.1 wasm32-unknown-unknown enables sign-ext and mutable-globals (in codegen since 1.70), multivalue and reference-types (default since 1.82, LLVM 19) and bulk-memory and nontrapping-fptoint (since 1.87, LLVM 20); simd128 and relaxed-simd are off. None of the six is float arithmetic: `f64 as i32` saturates the same with nontrapping-fptoint and bulk-memory switched off (checked), while every change to the default set changes module bytes. `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd` leaves the default set as it is and does not stop a function that enables relaxed-simd itself.
recipes.how: Read the set with `rustc +1.98.1 --print cfg --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` or `cfg!(target_feature = "...")`, and read what a built module used from its `target_features` custom section (the solver copy lists +bulk-memory, +bulk-memory-opt, +call-indirect-overlong, +multivalue, +mutable-globals, +nontrapping-fptoint, +reference-types, +sign-ext). For an MVP-only module on stable use wasm32v1-none (Tier 2 since 1.84; no std, only core and alloc; only mutable-globals); turning features off on wasm32-unknown-unknown does not rebuild the precompiled std, and a full MVP build needs nightly -Zbuild-std. Keep the -relaxed-simd pin in .cargo/config.toml and build.mjs, and add a cheap gate that the module's target_features section lists neither +relaxed-simd nor +simd128, beside T3's opcode lint.
recipes.rust_version: 1.70 (sign-ext, mutable-globals), 1.82 (multivalue, reference-types), 1.84 (wasm32v1-none Tier 2), 1.87 (bulk-memory, nontrapping-fptoint); measured on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: reference-types (1.82) changed call_indirect's table immediate to an over-long 5-byte LEB (the +call-indirect-overlong entry), which decoders without reference-types support reject. Enabling multivalue did not change the extern "C" ABI. The relaxed-SIMD intrinsics (e.g. core::arch::wasm32::f64x2_relaxed_madd) are stable since 1.82: a `#[target_feature(enable = "simd128,relaxed-simd")]` function compiles under `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd` (checked) and, in the scratch probe, emitted f64x2.relaxed_madd, recorded +relaxed-simd in target_features, and returned the fused result under node 22 on this x86 host (-8.67e-19 where a separate multiply and add give 0). On wasm such a function is callable without an unsafe block. Switching bulk-memory and nontrapping-fptoint off changed the probe's size (1591014 -> 1591189 bytes) but not its results.
recipes.engine_note: solver/.cargo/config.toml and solver/build.mjs both pass -C target-feature=-relaxed-simd; on 1.98.1 that flag changes nothing in the default set (checked), so it guards against a future default, while FLAGS.md's 'this build disables' does not cover a dependency function that opts in with #[target_feature] - only inspecting the module (T3's opcode lint, or the target_features section) catches that. A toolchain bump that changes the default set, as 1.82 and 1.87 did, changes the digest in fixtures/solver.sha256; the golden hash should not move for that reason.
recipes.verify_note: 7/7 oracle checks pass, incl. bitmask=63 (six on) and =2 (wasm32v1-none). Feature versions (1.70/1.82-LLVM19/1.87-LLVM20) confirmed on rustc book + dedicated blog + 1.70 RELEASES.md. Engine's -relaxed-simd pin confirmed twice.

recipes.name: Expect wasm32 undefined symbols to fail the link since 1.96 and the standard C ABI since 1.89
recipes.what: Since 1.96 rustc no longer passes --allow-undefined to wasm-ld, so an extern function with no definition is a link error ('undefined symbol') instead of a silent `env` import; since 1.89 `extern "C"` on wasm32-unknown-unknown follows the standard tool-conventions C ABI, which changed how aggregates are passed and left scalars alone; 1.84 removed the wasm32-wasi target name (now wasm32-wasip1) and added wasm32v1-none at Tier 2.
recipes.how: Declare each intended host import explicitly with `#[link(wasm_import_module = "env")]` (or another module name) on its `unsafe extern "C"` block; `-C link-arg=--allow-undefined` restores the old behaviour for a whole build. Keep exports scalar and pointer only (u32, f64, *const u8), which both ABIs lower the same way; a #[repr(C)] struct passed by value is passed indirectly under the 1.89+ ABI where the legacy ABI split it into separate parameters. Name WASI targets wasm32-wasip1 or wasm32-wasip2.
recipes.rust_version: 1.84 (wasm32-wasi removed, wasm32v1-none Tier 2), 1.89 (standard C ABI), 1.96 (no --allow-undefined); measured on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: Before 1.96 a misspelt or missing extern fn produced a module importing `env.<name>`, which a loader that instantiates with no import object discovered only at instantiation. 1.86 made the wasm_c_abi future-compatibility warning a hard error (it concerned wasm-bindgen older than 0.2.89). 1.91.0 broke #[link(wasm_import_module)] across crates (same-named imports from different modules could resolve to the wrong function); 1.91.1 fixed it.
recipes.engine_note: The solver declares no extern block and imports nothing (build.mjs instantiates with `new WebAssembly.Instance(module)` and no import object), so on 1.96+ an accidental undefined symbol fails `cargo build` instead of the JS instantiation. Its ten exports take u32/f64 and return u32/f64/pointers, the class the C ABI post says is unaffected. Keep T3's no-imports check as a second gate, and give T2's restore exports the same scalar/pointer signatures.
recipes.verify_note: 4/4 oracle checks pass. 1.96 link-error, 1.89 standard C ABI, 1.91.1 wasm_import_module fix all confirmed verbatim. Engine: no extern block, build.mjs instantiates with no import object (line 77), all 10 exports scalar/pointer-only.

recipes.name: Replace flat-buffer index math with 1.86-1.93 std APIs: as_chunks_mut, get_disjoint_mut, as_array
recipes.what: Stable std now covers what the solver does by hand: `<[T]>::as_chunks_mut::<N>()` (1.88) views a flat f64 buffer as `[[f64; N]]`, `get_disjoint_mut([i, j])` (1.86) hands out two records mutably and reports overlap as an `Err`, `<[T]>::as_array::<N>()` (1.93) turns a sub-slice into `&[T; N]`, `strict_add` and the other `strict_*` methods (1.91) panic on overflow even with overflow-checks off, `f64::midpoint` (1.85) and `next_up` / `next_down` (1.86) avoid overflow and epsilon tricks, `cfg_select!` (1.95) replaces cfg-if, and `floor` / `round` / `trunc` (const since 1.90) and `mul_add` (const since 1.94) work in constants.
recipes.how: Write `let (records, rest) = buf.as_chunks_mut::<BODY_STRIDE>(); debug_assert!(rest.is_empty());` and index `records[i][HX]`; take a pair with `let [a, b] = records.get_disjoint_mut([i, j])?;`; take a quaternion as `b[6..10].as_array::<4>()`; use `strict_*` where overflow is a bug (counts, offsets) and keep `wrapping_*` where wrap-around is intended (hash mixing); use `cfg_select!` for wasm-versus-native constants. Keep midpoint and mul_add out of law arithmetic: the law must repeat the JS kernel's exact operation sequence.
recipes.rust_version: 1.85-1.95 as listed per API; all present on the 1.98.1 pin
recipes.gotchas: `strict_*` ignores `overflow-checks = false` (checked: exit 101 under -C overflow-checks=off), so in the solver's panic = "abort" wasm build it becomes a trap; use it only where aborting is right. `get_disjoint_mut` also returns Err for an out-of-bounds index, and `as_chunks_mut` returns a remainder that must be checked. APIs newer than rust-toolchain.toml's pin fail to compile. Other additions in the period: LazyCell / LazyLock (1.80), Vec::extract_if (1.87), array_windows (1.94), Box::new_zeroed (1.92), core::hint::cold_path (1.95), assert_matches! (1.96, not in the prelude).
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs `body_at` / `field` and `resolve_pair(bodies, i, j)` (two bodies mutated through index arithmetic), rapier_law.rs `body_at` / `collider_at` copy loops and `quat_from_body(&b)` are the index-arithmetic sites; `mix_u64`'s wrapping_mul / wrapping_add must stay wrapping. Any such rewrite changes the digest (code and panic locations move) but should leave the golden hash unchanged; prove that with the three-engine golden run.
recipes.verify_note: 4/4 oracle checks pass. get_disjoint_mut/next_up 1.86, as_chunks_mut 1.88, strict_* 1.91, as_array 1.93, cfg_select! 1.95, midpoint 1.85, floor-const 1.90, mul_add-const 1.94 all confirmed on live std docs.

recipes.name: Keep 1.98's f64::algebraic_* methods out of the law: the std docs allow different results per run
recipes.what: 1.98 stabilized `algebraic_add`, `_sub`, `_mul`, `_div` and `_rem` on f32 and f64, which let the compiler combine and reorder operations, swap division for reciprocal multiplication and ignore the sign of zero; the core docs say the same inputs may produce different results even within one program run. They compile on stable with no feature gate and no warning (checked).
recipes.how: Keep the law to + - * / and sqrt, as lib.rs's header comment says, and keep algebraic_* (and mul_add) out of solver/src by review plus a CI grep for `algebraic_`. Constants may be computed by const fn since 1.82: `const SLIDE_ANGLE: f64 = radians(50.0)` has the same bits as the runtime call for this non-NaN expression (checked). Never hash a NaN's bits: f64::NAN is guaranteed quiet since 1.88, but its payload and sign may change across Rust versions and targets, and a NaN produced at compile time need not match the one produced at run time - reject or canonicalize first.
recipes.rust_version: algebraic_* 1.98; const-fn float arithmetic 1.82; NAN quiet guarantee 1.88
recipes.gotchas: A model trained before 1.98 calls these nightly-only; on 1.98.1 they are plain stable methods and nothing in rustc warns about them. The 1.82 announcement warns that `(0.0 / 0.0).is_sign_positive()` can differ between compile time and run time and across hardware, optimization level and surrounding code, and advises fully portable code to avoid to_bits and to test `f.signum() == 1.0` rather than `f.is_sign_positive()` (the advice concerns NaN results). No `algebraic_` appears in the pinned rapier3d-f64 0.35.3, parry3d-f64 0.30.2, nalgebra 0.35.0, simba 0.10.2, glam 0.33.10 or libm 0.2.16 sources (grep of the local cargo registry), so a dependency bump is where they could enter.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs computes CLIMB_ANGLE and SLIDE_ANGLE as consts; `bad` rejects NaN before `mix_f64` hashes `to_bits()`, and `canon_zero` passes NaN through untouched - the discipline the NaN notes require. Add `algebraic_` to the source lints that accompany T3's relaxed-SIMD opcode lint, and grep the Cargo.lock diff's crates for it on every dependency bump.
recipes.verify_note: 4/4 oracle checks pass. algebraic_* stabilization + reorder/non-determinism wording confirmed verbatim on 1.98.0 announcement and core f32 docs. Engine: canon_zero passes NaN through untouched, mix_f64 hashes to_bits() exactly as claimed.

recipes.name: Stop sorting floats with partial_cmp().unwrap_or(Equal): 1.81+ sorts panic on a non-total order
recipes.what: 1.81 replaced the slice sorts with driftsort (stable) and ipnsort (unstable), which may panic when the comparison is not a total order; the old 'NaN-tolerant' idiom `sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap_or(Ordering::Equal))` panics on 1.98.1 with 'user-provided comparison function does not correctly implement a total order' once a NaN is in a 64-element slice (checked), where older sorts silently returned some order.
recipes.how: Sort f64 keys with `total_cmp` (`v.sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b))`), which puts -0.0 before 0.0 and a positive NaN last (checked); better, reject NaN before sorting and sort by integer keys where they exist; keep PartialOrd and Ord consistent; never depend on which of several equal elements binary_search returns (1.82 changed it).
recipes.rust_version: 1.81+ (new sorts); binary_search change 1.82; BTreeMap::append 1.96; derive(PartialOrd) fast path 1.98
recipes.gotchas: The release note says 'may panic': detection is best-effort - a comparator that never returns Equal did not panic on a 200-element probe, so a passing test proves nothing. In the solver's panic = "abort" wasm build a sort panic is a trap. 1.96 made BTreeMap::append able to panic on incorrect Ord impls, and 1.98's derive(PartialOrd) fast path breaks types whose PartialOrd and Ord disagree.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `rebuild_snapshot` sorts contact pairs by `(collider1.into_raw_parts(), collider2.into_raw_parts())` - integer tuples, a total order, safe. Future sorts by f64 (T6 reachability sweep, T5 replay corpus ordering) should use total_cmp or integer keys, after NaN rejection.
recipes.verify_note: 2/2 oracle checks pass (NaN sort panics; total_cmp sorts cleanly). 1.81 panic wording, 1.82 binary_search change, 1.96 BTreeMap::append, 1.98 derive(PartialOrd) all confirmed verbatim. Engine's integer-tuple sort confirmed on main.

recipes.name: Gate solver CI with Cargo's build.warnings (1.97), not RUSTFLAGS, and keep --locked across resolver 3
recipes.what: Cargo 1.80-1.98 added knobs the solver build should use: `build.warnings` / CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS (1.97) denies local lint warnings without touching RUSTFLAGS; resolver "3" (1.84, implied by edition 2024) makes resolution MSRV-aware; check-cfg is always on (1.80); and cargo info (1.82), automatic cache GC (1.88), cargo fix using the build commands' target selection (1.89), publish --workspace (1.90), build.build-dir and `--target host-tuple` (1.91), config `include` and TOML 1.1 manifests (1.94) and resolver.lockfile-path (1.97).
recipes.how: In CI run the solver build as `CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny node solver/build.mjs --check` (or set `[build] warnings = "deny"` in solver/.cargo/config.toml). RUSTFLAGS outranks every config rustflags entry (order: CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS, RUSTFLAGS, target.<triple>/<cfg>.rustflags, build.rustflags), so a -Dwarnings placed in config is dropped whenever build.mjs sets RUSTFLAGS, while build.warnings is not a rustflag (measured: with build.mjs's RUSTFLAGS it failed the edition-2021 copy on its 7 warnings: 'warnings are denied by `build.warnings` configuration'). Keep building with --locked so an edition bump's resolver 3 cannot move Cargo.lock (measured: the edition-2024 copy built with --locked --offline and an unchanged lock). Declare any custom cfg in `[lints.rust] unexpected_cfgs` check-cfg so the 1.80 lint stays quiet.
recipes.rust_version: Cargo 1.80-1.98 per knob as listed; measured with cargo 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: build.warnings covers only lint warnings from local packages, not dependency or non-lint warnings. Config `include` accepts only paths ending in .toml. Automatic GC deletes downloaded crates unused for about three months and does not run under --offline or --frozen, so an offline rebuild of an old commit may need a fetch first. TOML 1.1 syntax in Cargo.toml raises the development MSRV (Cargo parses TOML 1.1 from 1.94), though published manifests stay readable by older parsers. With incompatible-rust-versions = "fallback" the resolver only prefers compatible versions; with none available it still picks one.

lanes.verifier_note: Checked all 49 warrant sources by direct retrieval (Rust Reference/Book/Nomicon/std docs on doc.rust-lang.org, 6 version-announcement blog posts, RFC 2451, PR rust-lang/rust#133372, lang-team issue #286, and 4 rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 docs.rs source files) and every engine_note claim against the live si-rpg-engine repo (solver/src/lib.rs, solver/src/rapier_law.rs, solver/Cargo.toml, solver/Cargo.lock, docs/dispatch-t2-restore.md) via gh api. I also ran all 77 of the lane's checks myself through scripts/compile_oracle.py against the real pinned rustc 1.98.1 with rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 / parry3d-f64 0.30.2 exactly as locked in Cargo.lock: 77/77 passed, reproducing rustc's exact wording verbatim ("is not dyn compatible", "missing required bound on `Item`" with no code, the literal `DVec3` name in the E0117 note for Rapier's Vector, "required for `Log` to implement `MaybeSync`", "is a \"sealed trait\"", "the struct `Cell<T>` is invariant..."). No source misattribution, no stale API, no check/prose mismatch, and no engine-fact error found in any of the 10 recipes. Systemic weakness: several softening "gotchas" clauses are asserted but not independently exercised by that recipe's own checks[] — recipe 1 claims associated consts and GATs make a trait dyn-incompatible with no check of its own (only recipe 2's checks demonstrate it), and recipe 9 claims a sealed trait still permits calling its public methods from outside without ever demonstrating that call. A reader who trusted only checks[] as ground truth would not catch a regression in these secondary claims.

recipes.name: Choose associated types for one-impl-per-type outputs; enforce associated consts and GATs at compile time
recipes.what: An associated type fixes one output per implementing type (a second impl is E0119) while a generic parameter allows many impls; an associated const is evaluated only when an instantiated path references it; generic associated types (stable since 1.65) let an associated type borrow from self.
recipes.how: Use `trait Law { type Input; const STRIDE: usize; ... }` when each implementor has exactly one natural choice (the Book's `Iterator::Item` argument). Use a generic parameter (`trait Integrate<T>`) when one type must serve several (f32 and f64), and disambiguate with `<Euler as Integrate<f64>>::integrate(&e, ..)`. Defaults shorten impls: `const ID: i32 = 1;` in the trait, `trait Add<Rhs = Self>`. Put an invariant on an associated const as `const STRIDE_OK: () = assert!(Self::STRIDE > 0, "...");` and reference it (`let () = Self::STRIDE_OK;`) inside the method that relies on it: an impl that violates it fails the build with E0080 ('evaluation panicked: ...') as soon as that method is instantiated. For a lending iterator write a GAT: `type Item<'a> where Self: 'a; fn next<'a>(&'a mut self) -> Option<Self::Item<'a>>;` so each item may be `&'a mut [f64]` into the iterator's own buffer, which `Iterator` cannot express.
recipes.gotchas: The `where Self: 'a` on a GAT is mandatory whenever a method signature proves it (`&'a mut self` returning `Self::Item<'a>`); leaving it off is a hard error, 'missing required bound on `Item`', with no error code. An associated-const assert only fires on a path the build instantiates: the same `STRIDE = 0` impl compiles in a binary that never calls `stride()` on it, and in a library whose only caller is private dead code; it fails once `main`, a test or a `pub fn` reaches it. A generic associated const cannot size an array on stable (`[f64; L::STRIDE]` is 'generic parameters may not be used in const operations'). Associated consts and GATs each make the trait dyn-incompatible. The GAT stabilization post lists known limits: an implied 'static requirement from higher-ranked bounds such as `for<'a> I::Item<'a>: Debug`, and borrow-checker false errors with lending iterators.
recipes.engine_note: If the solver grows a Law trait, `const STRIDE: usize` plus an assert-const is how BODY_STRIDE = 17 and COLLIDER_STRIDE = 10 (solver/src/lib.rs) become per-law compile-time facts. A concrete path still sizes the static buffers (`[f64; 64 * <BoxLaw as Law>::STRIDE]` is 1088 elements), but code generic over `L: Law` cannot declare `[f64; L::STRIDE]` on stable, so the buffers stay concrete arrays.
recipes.verify_note: 10/10 checks pass on live rustc 1.98.1 (oracle run), incl. instantiation-only const-eval (4 variants) and GAT no-code error verbatim. BODY_STRIDE=17/COLLIDER_STRIDE=10/MAX_BODIES=64 confirmed in solver/src/lib.rs.

recipes.name: Keep a trait dyn compatible or fence methods with `where Self: Sized`; a &dyn is two words: data + vtable
recipes.what:
A trait can be a `dyn` base only if its supertraits are dyn compatible, `Sized` is not a supertrait, it has no associated consts and no GATs, and each method is dispatchable (no type parameters, `Self` only in the receiver `&self`/`&mut self`/`Box`/`Rc`/`Arc`/`Pin

`, no `async fn`, no `-> impl Trait`) or is excluded by `where Self: Sized`; otherwise E0038, which on 1.98.1 reads 'the trait `X` is not dyn compatible' (formerly 'object safety').
recipes.how: Audit a trait against the Reference list before writing `&dyn Trait` or `Box<dyn Trait>`. Move generic helpers behind `where Self: Sized`: they stay callable on concrete types and leave the vtable. Pointers to DSTs are twice a thin pointer: `&dyn T`, `Box<dyn T>` and `&[f64]` are `2 * size_of::<usize>()`, i.e. 16 bytes on x86_64 and 8 on wasm32, holding the data pointer plus a vtable pointer (trait objects) or a length (slices, str). The vtable holds one function pointer per method of the trait and its supertraits. Write `T: ?Sized` on a type parameter to accept `str`, `[f64]` or `dyn Trait` behind a reference (trait `Self` is already `?Sized`). `Box<dyn T>` means `Box<dyn T + 'static>`; a trait object that borrows needs `Box<dyn T + '_>`.
recipes.rust_version: any; the 'dyn compatible' wording is what 1.98.1 prints
recipes.gotchas: Calling a `where Self: Sized` method on a trait object fails with 'the `visit` method cannot be invoked on a trait object' (no error code). Adding a generic method, an associated const, a GAT, an `async fn` or an RPIT method to a trait that is used as `dyn` breaks every `dyn` user. Older docs and crates say 'object safe'; the diagnostic changed from 'cannot be made into an object' in rust-lang/rust#133372 (merged 2025-01-22, milestone 1.86.0), following the lang-team rename proposal. Returning `Box<dyn Probe>` built from a borrowing type fails with 'lifetime may not live long enough' because of the implicit 'static. Fat-pointer sizes are per target: never hard-code 16 in code that also builds for wasm32.
recipes.engine_note: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 puts dynamic dispatch on the solver's path: `PhysicsWorld::step()` is `self.step_with_events(&(), &())` with parameters `hooks: &dyn PhysicsHooks, events: &dyn EventHandler`, and `warm_broadphase` in solver/src/rapier_law.rs passes `&(), &()` to `CollisionPipeline::step`, with `()` as the no-op implementor. The solver's own `step` and `resolve_pair` (solver/src/lib.rs) use no trait objects; on wasm32 each fat pointer is two 32-bit words.

recipes.name: Apply the whole orphan rule: a local type before any uncovered type parameter, and no overlapping impls
recipes.what: For `impl<P1..=Pn> Trait<T1..=Tn> for T0` with a foreign trait, one of T0..=Tn must be local and no uncovered type parameter may appear before the first local one (RFC 2451); `&`, `&mut`, `Box` and `Pin` are fundamental, so `&Local` and `Box<Local>` count as local; overlapping impls are E0119, including overlap that only a future upstream impl could create.
recipes.how: Read the error code: E0117 = foreign trait on only foreign types (`impl Display for Vec<f64>`, `impl From<[f64; 17]> for rapier3d_f64::prelude::Vector`) — wrap in a local newtype or record type; E0210 = uncovered type parameter before the first local type (`impl<T> From<Snapshot> for T`); E0119 = overlap. Shapes that pass: `impl<T> From<Snapshot> for Vec<T>` (T covered by Vec, Snapshot local), `impl Display for Box<Snapshot>` and `impl From<&BodyRecord> for Vector` (fundamental wrappers of a local type). A blanket impl `impl<T: Display> Describe for T` claims every type that can ever satisfy the bound: add specific impls only for local types that do not meet it.
recipes.gotchas: The one-sentence rule ('the trait or the type must be local') is incomplete: `impl<T> From<Snapshot> for T` names a local type and still fails with E0210. Coherence reasons about the future: next to `impl<T: Display> Describe for T`, `impl Describe for Vec<u8>` is E0119 today even though `Vec<u8>` is not Display ('upstream crates may add a new impl of trait `std::fmt::Display`...'), while the same pair for a local non-Display type compiles. Rapier's `Vector` is glam's `DVec3` at 0.35.3 (rustc names it in the E0117 note), so it is foreign to the solver crate.
recipes.engine_note: Conversions between the solver's stride-17 body records (solver/src/lib.rs) and Rapier values must go through a local type: `impl From<[f64; 17]> for Vector` is E0117, `impl From<&BodyRecord> for Vector` with a local `BodyRecord` compiles and converts (the BodyRecord check prints `0 1.5 0`).

recipes.name: Let auto traits follow the fields, steer them with PhantomData, and know a Drop impl drives drop check
recipes.what: Send, Sync, Unpin, UnwindSafe and RefUnwindSafe are auto traits: a struct gets one when all its fields have it, and stable code cannot write negative impls; `PhantomData<*const ()>` removes Send and Sync, `PhantomData<fn() -> T>` keeps a typed handle Send + Sync whatever T is, and since RFC 1238 a `PhantomData<T>` field is superfluous for drop check when the type has an explicit Drop impl: the Drop impl itself makes drop check strict, while the phantom still sets variance and auto traits.
recipes.how: Assert auto traits in code: `fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}` then `assert_send::<MyType>();` (E0277 names the field that breaks it). Choose the phantom from the Nomicon table: `PhantomData<T>` (owns T, covariant, inherits Send/Sync), `PhantomData<fn() -> T>` (covariant, always Send + Sync: typed ids and handles), `PhantomData<*const ()>` (!Send + !Sync), `PhantomData<fn(T) -> T>` (invariant). `size_of::<PhantomData<T>>() == 0` is guaranteed, so `Handle<Body> { index: u32, _for: PhantomData<fn() -> Body> }` is 4 bytes and a `Handle<Collider>` passed where `Handle<Body>` is wanted is E0308. A marker trait can require an auto trait for all implementors: rapier's `pub trait MaybeSync: Sync {}` with `impl<T: Sync + ?Sized> MaybeSync for T {}`, used as a supertrait.
recipes.gotchas: Common wrong advice: 'add PhantomData<T> for drop check'. The Nomicon: since RFC 1238 an extra `PhantomData<T>` is superfluous for dropck when the type has a Drop impl (it still sets variance and auto traits), and the std docs warn its drop-check interaction may change. What makes `inspector = Inspector(&days)` fail with E0597 ('...when `inspector` is dropped and runs the `Drop` code for type `Inspector`') is the Drop impl: without it the same code compiles. `Rc`, `RefCell` and raw pointers remove Send/Sync from every struct that contains them, and you find out at the bound, not at the field.
recipes.engine_note: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 declares `pub trait EventHandler: crate::utils::MaybeSync`, and `MaybeSync: Sync` unless the crate's `unsync-callbacks` feature is enabled, which solver/Cargo.toml does not do. A solver-side collision log therefore must be Sync: a `RefCell<u32>` counter is E0277 ('required for `Log` to implement `MaybeSync`'), an `AtomicU32` compiles (the AtomicU32 check drops a box onto a slab for 64 quanta at dt = 1/64 with `step_with_events(&(), &log)` and counts 1 started collision). Typed `Handle<T>` wrappers over the body and collider indices would keep the stride-17 and stride-10 buffers apart at zero bytes.

recipes.name: Choose variance on purpose: &'a T, Box and Vec are covariant; &mut T and Cell invariant; fn(T) contravariant
recipes.what: Rust subtyping is over lifetimes (`&'static str` is a subtype of `&'a str`); covariant constructors pass it through (`&'a T`, `*const T`, `[T]`, `fn() -> T`, `PhantomData<T>`, Box, Vec), `fn(T)` flips it, and `&'a mut T` (in T), `*mut T`, `UnsafeCell<T>`/`Cell<T>` and `dyn Trait<T>` (in T) forbid it; a struct takes the combination of its fields, and a parameter used both ways becomes invariant.
recipes.how: Expect invariance wherever a type can write a T: `fn assign<T>(input: &mut T, val: T)` called with `&mut hello` (a `&'static str`) forces `T = &'static str`, so passing `&world` is E0597. Rely on covariance to shorten lifetimes (`Box<&'static str>` to `Box<&'a str>`, `Vec<&'static str>` to `Vec<&'a str>`). A sink `fn(&'a str)` may stand where `fn(&'static str)` is expected, never the reverse (E0521). In your own generic types choose with PhantomData: `PhantomData<fn(&'id ()) -> &'id ()>` makes `'id` invariant, a brand the compiler will not shrink. rustc's notes name the culprit: 'the struct `Cell<T>` is invariant over the parameter `T`'.
recipes.gotchas: Invariance errors surface far from the cause, as 'does not live long enough' (E0597) or 'lifetime may not live long enough' (no code), because an annotation such as `&'static str` pinned the lifetime. Putting a `Cell`, `RefCell` or `&mut` of a borrowed type inside a long-lived struct makes that struct invariant, which then refuses ordinary shortening. `dyn Trait<T> + 'a` is covariant in 'a but invariant in T.

recipes.name: Write for<'a> bounds when a generic must accept a borrow that the function creates itself
recipes.what: A lifetime parameter on a function is chosen by the caller and outlives the call, so it cannot name a borrow of a local; a higher-ranked bound (`F: for<'a> Fn(&'a f64) -> f64`, or the elided `Fn(&f64) -> f64`, or `where for<'a> &'a C: IntoIterator<Item = &'a f64>`) must hold for every lifetime, including that local one.
recipes.how: When a generic calls a closure on data the function owns or borrows internally, write the bound elided (`F: Fn(&f64) -> f64`) or explicit (`F: for<'a> Fn(&'a f64) -> f64`); the Reference expands elided Fn-trait lifetimes to `for<'a>`. To iterate any collection by reference: `fn sum_all<C>(c: C) -> f64 where for<'a> &'a C: IntoIterator<Item = &'a f64>` serves `Vec<f64>`, `[f64; N]` and `VecDeque<f64>` with one body. `for<'a>` may prefix the whole bound (`for<'a> F: Fn(&'a i32)`) or just the trait; only the scope of the name differs.
recipes.gotchas: The tempting fix of adding `<'a>` to the function (`fn sum_all<'a, C: 'a>(c: C) where &'a C: IntoIterator<..>`) fails with E0597 ('`c` does not live long enough'), because `'a` must outlive the whole call. Elided lifetimes in `Fn(&T) -> &U` bounds and in `fn(&T)` pointer types are already higher-ranked; `for<'a>` must be written out for non-Fn traits such as `&'a C: IntoIterator`.
recipes.verify_note: 4/4 checks pass on rustc 1.98.1, incl. E0597 for both the naive fn-level 'a attempt and confirming the for<'a>-bound fix compiles. No engine_note; foundational HRTB knowledge not yet applied in solver code.
